Our primary tool involves a novel, streamlined version of the Rokhlin cocycle theorem tailored to Potyagailo's general framework for cocycles.

The study of dust formation in the early universe is complicated by the limited availability of direct observational data on dust levels at very distant cosmological ages.  A team of researchers developed a method to indirectly assess the amount of dust present in the universe at z=5.69 by analyzing the properties of a massive molecular cloud, known as GN20.  This massive cloud at the center of a galaxy hosts a massive black hole and features a large superbubble formed by the expulsion of gas by the galaxy's central engine.  Analyzing near-infrared light from GN20 allowed the researchers to create a three-dimensional map of the dust content within the superbubble.  To estimate the amount of dust present, the team accounted for the effects of various processes such as the formation of pair-instability and core-collapse supernovae, as well as dust dispersal resulting from massive star interactions, to determine the initial dust budget within the cloud.  The amount of dust produced through these processes was compared to the amount of dust observed within the superbubble to provide a measure of the dust levels present in the universe at a given cosmological age.  The findings showed that the amount of dust produced through pair-instability and core-collapse supernovae, as well as dust reaccumulation following the dissolution of massive stars' systems, accounted for the majority of dust present within the cloud.  The results also enabled the estimation of the dust production rate within GN20 in comparison to other galaxies across varying cosmological ages.

To enhance the safety of autonomous vehicles by improving their 3D object detection capabilities on highways, this research introduces a novel, two-stage approach for combining RGB and lidar data.  Firstly, a detection network is applied to each individual RGB and lidar dataset separately, resulting in two sets of 3D bounding box predictions.  Secondly, two intermediate feature maps from the two networks are fused using a cross-sensor fusion module, allowing the exchange of semantic and spatial information between RGB and lidar features.  Objects with predicted probabilities above a certain threshold are selectively fused with the cross-sensor fusion module, while the remaining predictions undergo a non-maximum suppression technique to minimize redundant detections.  A separate evaluation of the research was conducted using the Baidu Apollo dataset, showing improved results for far-field 3D object detection compared to current state-of-the-art methods.  Code and dataset available at: https://github.com/Trigiant/fcfc4.git

A newly developed classical reverse amplitude optimization (RAO) algorithm was combined with a quantum learning machine (QLM) to efficiently generate complex molecular states. The RAO's ability to train the QLM was tested by using it to create a wide range of one- and two-particle excitation states on the N2 molecule, comparing the results to conventional methods. By comparing energy spectra and observables, the accuracy of the hybrid approach was validated. This combination of classical optimization and quantum learning also demonstrated an important ability to overcome issues with vanishing amplitudes in minimal models.

During laparoscopic surgery, tracking the organ's actual position and layout in relation to preoperative planning images is crucial.  The process of mapping preoperative images to actual intraoperative conditions has been shown to be effective using organ models and vision-based methods.  One major challenge in this process is accounting for the discrepancies that inevitably arise during surgery.  We are addressing this issue by developing a new method to correct organ models based on their performance in real-time intraoperative data, specifically during surgery.  We have tested this approach on two different surgical procedures - hysterectomy and cholecystectomy - using organ models derived from CT and MRI scans.  Our results show significant improvements in tracking accuracy with minimal computational costs.  Our method has been found to be particularly effective in situations with poor lighting and when there are significant shifts in the organ's position.  We have also found that it can be an useful tool for surgeons, taking just over one second to produce accurate tracking results.  Our code is available for public use on GitHub.

This study explores conformal matter collineations in degenerate spacetimes characterized by an irreducible energy-momentum tensor. The research determines the order of conformal matter collineations in such spaces, establishing their degree of freedom based on various tensor derivatives and degeneracy conditions. The analysis distinguishes between collineations with zero, four, eight, or sixteen degrees of freedom, corresponding to scenarios where the conformal metric is constant, has an associated Killing vector, is rigid but not necessarily Lorentzian, or possesses no transitive symmetry, respectively. The study further illustrates the degree of freedom for non-rotating, static, and U(1)-symmetric spacetimes. The research also demonstrates the application of conformal matter collineations in simplifying the Einstein-Conformal Factor field equations under certain static and non-rotating conditions.

Estimating optical flow in real-world scenarios is highly prone to errors due to common occlusions. To overcome this limitation, many recent approaches have used self-supervised training, which has yielded impressive results even without labeled data. However, existing self-supervised methods consistently struggle with occluded areas, as they leverage the assumption that flow is continuous across the entire image. To break past this limitation, we've developed a novel self-supervised optical flow estimation model, capable of learning from easily obtainable non-occluded patches. By training the model using these patches, we've shown significant gains of up to 2.5 times in error reduction in Flow++'s benchmark tests for occluded areas, with only a minor decrease in performance on unobstructed areas. Our findings demonstrate that learning from non-occluded patches is an effective technique for improving self-supervised flow estimation, particularly in areas with occlusions.

Deep learning techniques have significantly transformed the classification of features in various fields, delivering exceptional performance. Nonetheless, the energy efficiency of neural network-based classification systems remains a critical concern. To address this issue, we present a compact, general-purpose classifier using sparse logistic regression-based neural networks. Our model surpasses traditional ANN-based classifiers in accuracy across multiple datasets while achieving a substantial 5-7 times lower test accuracy on CPU and 2-3 times lower test accuracy on GPU. Additionally, our classifier demonstrates adaptability by accurately predicting features in diverse real-world applications, including gender classification in faces, malicious traffic detection in network data, and predicting forest cover types from cartographic attributes. The code and model are openly accessible on CodaLab for reproducibility and further development.

This research investigates the effects of a strong magnetic field on spin polarized strange quark matter, examining its under pressure behavior and comparing it to the behavior of spin polarized strange quark matter in a strong magnetic field. To accomplish this, the Dirac equation is employed to determine the energy spectrum of quarks within a strong magnetic field, and the relativistic mean-field theory is applied to quarks to develop an equation of state for spin polarized strange quark matter under pressure. The calculated results demonstrate that a strong magnetic field can induce symmetry energy in spin polarized strange quark matter, causing its density to become greater than that of normal spin polarized strange quark matter. Additionally, the structure of massive stars composed of spin polarized strange quark matter within a strong magnetic field is explored, including the relationship between their density, radius, and magnetic field strength. The findings also indicate that a strong magnetic field can increase the neutron star's magnetic field strength, as well as its rotational period, while decreasing its surface temperature.

A notable property called even-2-factorability (E2F) is introduced in this study, requiring a cubic graph to have an even 2-factor consisting of two edge-disjoint components. This property is highly sought after because it guarantees the presence of an Eulerian circuit. While the property is highly desirable, very few cubic graphs meet the even-2-factorability criterion. In this research, we identify several classes of cubic graphs that naturally satisfy even-2-factorability, as well as determine the specific structure of these graphs. Additionally, we present a method for determining whether a given cubic graph meets the even-2-factorability condition, essentially resolving the long-standing question of whether any cubic graph can be classified as even-2-factorable. This resolution is achieved through the identification of a particular cubic graph, the prism graph obtained by connecting every vertex of a given graph, which serves as the basis for constructing an even-2-factor in any cubic graph.

In this study, we make significant progress in analyzing the frequency of prime values taken by a specific family of quadratic polynomials, of the form $ax^2+bx+c$. By establishing a bound for the adelic prime count, we can determine that at least $O(x^{2-\varepsilon})$ prime values are below $x$ for this family of quadratic polynomials, with the additional restriction that the coefficients $a, b, c$ are relatively prime and $a$ is negative. This finding supplements and expands upon Li's modified Bateman-Horn Conjecture, which posits that there are at least $x^{2-\varepsilon}$ prime values below or up to $x$ for this family of quadratic polynomials, with no additional constraints on the coefficients. Our results also provide a significant advancement in this area of research. Additionally, our work on the bound for the adelic prime count leads to several interesting applications and implications, including an investigation into the behavior of twin primes and the distribution of primes in arithmetic progressions.

This paper introduces a novel technique called Timeloops, a system call filtering framework that allows applications written in interpreted languages, such as PHP, Python, and JavaScript, to have system call access control enabled. Unlike compiled languages like C and C++, which can have system calls directly compiled into machine code, interpreted languages use dynamic method calls to access system functions from a runtime environment. Timeloops overcomes this challenge by leveraging the interactivity of these languages with their runtime environments to dynamically intercept and filter system calls. We show that this approach allows us to effectively monitor and manage system calls made by these applications. Additionally, we highlight the limitations of previous system call monitoring approaches and present a design for a Timeloops framework, along with a prototype implementation of a Python runtime environment called Pyloopy, which enables system call access control for Python applications. We also conduct a feasibility study of applying the Timeloops approach to other interpreted languages, including JavaScript and Ruby, and present a case study of a system call monitoring demonstration featuring Python applications.

This research focuses on a type of dark matter denoted as $a_0$ that is based on a pseudo-Goldstone boson and arises from an electroweak symmetric multiplet containing the $\pi^0$, $etac$, and $eta'$ mesons. As a pseudo-Goldstone boson, its interaction with nucleons is weakened by a factor of $O(10^{-3})$ due to the chiral effective field theory, making its direct detection significantly more challenging. Nonetheless, despite these weakened interactions, the a0 particle still darkens the amygdala region of parameter space that is difficult to access with other direct detection methods. Nonetheless, the a0 particle's weakened nucleon interactions also make it more susceptible to constraints from nuclear processes such as stellar cooling, the mole dissolution rate of certain substances, and the mole dissolution rate of certain substances, the mole dissolution rate of Pauli exclusion principle, and X-ray observations of galaxy clusters, all of which the a0 particle fails to conform to. Moreover, the a0 particle's weakened nucleon interactions also make it more susceptible to constraints from nuclear processes such as stellar cooling, the mole dissolution rate of certain substances, the mole dissolution rate of Pauli exclusion principle, and X-ray observations of galaxy clusters, all of which the a0 particle fails to conform to.

To speed up the solution to target tracking problems where some targets aren't detected and have limited field of view, we've developed a new efficient method for calculating the number of undetected targets. This approach, based on recursive Bayesian estimation, uses prior information about the targets' locations and develops a set of feasible hypotheses to compute the upper limit of undetected targets quickly, without needing to check all possible combinations. By only considering the most plausible targets and using the detected observations, we've shown that our method can significantly reduce the computational complexity from cubic to quadratic, making it more suitable for real-time applications with numerous targets. We've tested and compared our method with the current state-of-the-art approach, Cloosterman's, using synthetic and real-world data, including the Scalable Scenarios Dataset, and found it to be more efficient and accurate.

This research paper examines the dynamics of a recent migration model that features delay, which was previously studied in a non-delayed migration model. We analyze the observability inequality of the model and employ it to investigate the exponential stability of an unobservable system. Additionally, we leverage the inequality to demonstrate the conditions under which the model's population exhibits extinction, and these conditions are expressed in terms of the migration delay, export coefficient, and the spectral properties of the system matrix. We illustrate the theoretical findings with numerical examples.

In high-stakes soccer matches, decisions made by players have far-reaching consequences, influencing the direction of the game. To gain insights into these choices, we must consider the underlying probability distributions governing the outcomes of actions, which in turn are affected by the specific situation in the game. Unfortunately, current methods that evaluate actions are often based on intuitive reasoning and lack a quantitative basis. To address this limitation, we have been collecting large datasets of professional soccer games along with the decisions made by players, including whether they chose to shoot on goal. By analyzing these datasets, we have determined the expected value of various actions such as committing a foul, causing the ball to go out of bounds, or making a pass, with the standard being whether they are more or less valuable than attempting a shot on goal. Furthermore, we have identified factors that influence the probability distributions of these actions and the resulting outcomes. For example, we found that players are more likely to shoot on goal in scenarios where the scoring opportunities are better, which aligns with their intuitive judgment. By quantifying the expected value of actions and the probability distributions governing the outcomes, we have established a framework that allows for the evaluation of decision-making strategies in soccer.

High-resolution subsurface imaging can be achieved through Full Waveform Inversion (FWI), which models forward and inverse problems using the physics of seismic wave propagation.
Although time-domain data representations offer intuitive physical connections with the recorded seismic signals, the FWI method typically produces distorted time-domain wavefields due to the non-linear relationship between time and frequency domain representations.
This study develops an alternative objective function that maintains the time-domain wavefield representation, allowing the optimization process to converge to the correct time-domain model without the need for frequency-domain approximations.
By bypassing the time-to-frequency domain transformation, the new method reduces computational costs associated with Fourier transforms and their inverse operations.
The proposed approach is tested using synthetic numerical examples that demonstrate its superior performance and greater flexibility when compared to existing frequency-domain FWI strategies.

Photonic systems that are based on resonator coupling and feature nonreciprocal behavior when optically controlled have advanced the capability of all-optical diode and quasi-circulator designs. However, the conventional method of achieving chiral coupling uses an asymmetrical design which complicates the manufacturing process. This discovery leverages chiral coupling between identical resonators to create a nonreciprocal effect by utilizing a gyrotropic metamaterial fill, allowing for the construction of all-optical diodes and quasi-circulators without the need for asymmetry. Notably, this approach broadens the applications of these devices as it prevents the polarization of light from becoming stuck, enabling the operation of quasi-circulators even with high input power. Numerical modeling demonstrates the performance of these devices when using a high-temperature ferrite and a gyrotropic metamaterial with a high axial ratio.

We performed a thorough examination of IGRB J19294+1816, which exhibited its highest intensity in November 2019, observing it with the INGRID six-detector array, the AstroSat suite of three instruments, and the MAXI/GSC. By analyzing its pre-outburst spectrum from 2005 to 2019, we determined its average energy spectrum, which combines data from AstroSat's calorimeter and gas pixel detector on board AstroSat, showing a spectral pattern consistent with an absorbed power-law model. We discovered spectral characteristics such as a high energy logarithmic slope and a low interstellar absorption value during the outburst. Quasi-periodic Exponential Spectral Flints were found in the 2019 data, with an oscillatory period of approximately one day. The source's radial velocity was determined to be between -4.2 and -5.3 E+16 Hz, while its spin period was estimated to be around 1.56 to 1.63 seconds, with an error margin of up to 0.07 seconds. The direction of its spin axis was identified as 1.38 degrees ± 0.18 in right ascension and 69.85 degrees ± 0.17 in declination.

This study examines an asymmetric noisy voter model, where two species compete for dominance in a spatial environment. The model deviates from standard noisy voter models in two key aspects: species can change their type through a migration mechanism, influenced by an asymmetric external force, and there is a non-invasive type that can interact with other types in a symmetrical manner. The model is analyzed in a finite and infinite lattice under no initial order condition, and Monte Carlo simulations are employed to determine the impact of noise, asymmetry, and the migration rate on system dynamics. The findings indicate that the model exhibits robust coexistence, alternating order, and uniform order states, depending on the values of asymptotic mean drift, noise, and migration.

Indonesia, being a vast multi-cultural country with 18 provinces, has numerous sundials that remain undocumented. These ancient time-telling devices hold historical significance and can provide valuable geographical and temporal insights if properly recorded and analyzed. However, sundials are often destroyed or damaged due to lack of maintenance and knowledge about their existence. To address this issue, the Indonesian National Commission for UNESCO, in collaboration with local universities and international organizations, initiated the 'Citizen Science for Sundials' project. This project leverages online platforms and social media to raise public awareness about sundials and encourage citizens to contribute to their documentation through photo and video submissions. In addition, the project allows participants to report any damaged or destroyed sundials, providing a comprehensive dataset for further research and development. This project not only helps preserve sundials but also empowers citizens to engage in science and promote cultural awareness among the general public.

This paper investigates the secret key generation potential in DED2D systems, focusing on a scenario where data and energy are transferred from an encoder to multiple users with different reception capabilities. A novel TFIET scheme is proposed, involving time division and coding techniques to separate and secure the data and energy transfer to each user. An individual key generation process is applied to each user, with the aim of improving the security without compromising the energy efficiency. Our analysis first determines the secure key generation capacity for each user, followed by optimization of the TFIET scheme to maximize this capacity. Numerical results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed scheme in achieving high secure key rates for up to four users with different channel conditions, outperforming previously suggested systems.

The COVID19 pandemic has significantly accelerated the shift to remote work, causing numerous experiments and data collections to be conducted from home. As a result, there has been an increased need for automated setup automation in experiments. We have developed an innovative system that utilizes multi-agent reinforcement learning for the automated configuration of an experimental setup consisting of various devices generating random signals. Our system allows us to tranfer learning from a simulated environment to a real-world setup, streamlining the process of designing new setups. We have demonstrated the effectiveness of our approach by successfully automating the setup of an experimental signal processing system, comprising of analog devices capable of generating time-domain signals. Our findings show that our method can efficiently learn to optimize setup performance within the desired specifications, outperforming a random baseline by at least one order of magnitude. Additionally, our system excels in handling unexpected component failures during the learning process, achieving a significant improvement of at least two orders of magnitude in performance over the baseline in such scenarios.

In electron microscopy, electrostatic phase plates play a significant role in enhancing image contrast. Various design options for these plates, influenced by pixel pattern, size, and arrangement, can impact the formation of electron probes, resulting in changes to probe size and current density, which in turn affect the performance of image contrast enhancement. This study presents a computational method for evaluating the electron probe formed by a phase plate, taking into account the effects of electron source size, bohr radius, and the plate's design parameters. Using this approach, we investigated how different design features, such as fill-factor and pixel pattern, contribute to the electron probe's shape and current density, and demonstrated how these factors relate to the plate's transfer function. Our findings are applied to a specific image contrast enhancement technique to illustrate the influence of design parameters on the outcome. The developed method is a useful tool for optimizing the design of electrostatic phase plates based on the specific requirements of the electron source used.

Recent advances in dialogue understanding tasks are largely attributed to the application of deep learning models, specifically Sequence-to-Sequence architectures, for structured tasks and simple classification using Recurrent Neural Networks. Despite their success, these approaches are often hampered by reliance on extensive training data and labeled datasets. To address this limitation, a transfer learning framework is proposed, leveraging pre-trained Transformer-based models for tasks like sentiment analysis, aspect extraction, and dialog classification on the DSTC7 dataset. The proposed approach involves fine-tuning these models on smaller labeled datasets. Experimental results show that the transfer learning-based architectures outperform standalone RNN-based systems on multiple tasks, with the lowest error rate reduced by over 50% in some cases.

This paper presents a novel attention-based deep learning model that significantly enhances the detection of loop closures in images, a crucial aspect of building persistent and navigable maps in real-world, dynamically changing environments. By incorporating an attention mechanism that focuses on visual distinctions, we significantly improve the performance of our network, especially when confronted with diverse and ever-changing conditions. We present comprehensive experimental results utilizing the NuScenes dataset, demonstrating that our attention-based network outperforms cutting-edge segmentation models and robust approaches tailored to changing environments. Notably, when subjected to synthetic scenes that test the network's ability to generalize across diverse settings, our results show that a single trained model can effectively navigate through various scenarios with just a 10% reduction in performance, in comparison to a model tailored specifically to that environment. This achievement serves as a foundation for future research aimed at developing a fully generalizable map construction framework.

Mobile devices streaming high-quality video over 5G networks necessitates a robust and adaptable video delivery system. To ensure optimal viewing experience, a dynamic system is required to monitor performance and make data-driven decisions in real-time. A novel, hybrid video delivery model combines cloud and edge computing resources to maintain desired quality. This model utilizes Maximum Expected Utility theory to optimize quality settings, taking into account performance and energy considerations, across both cloud and edge domains. A real-world implementation, leveraging Amazon Web Services and Microsoft Azure, was developed to monitor the system's performance. This was achieved through the integration of open-source cloud and edge platforms, as well as purpose-built video streaming applications. In-depth testing, conducted over a commercial wireless network, demonstrated the system's capability to maintain optimal quality under varying network conditions. Furthermore, this was accomplished without compromising user quality of experience or necessitating advanced network knowledge.

To incorporate interactions in doped graphene, we develop a self-consistent theory adjusting the Dirac dispersion and carrying it through to its consequences. First, we determine the renormalized quasiparticle velocity using the Fermi distribution and a cutoff for interaction strength, then establish a general expression for the renormalized velocity in the strong-coupling regime. Next, we analyze the effect of renormalization on the renormalized velocity's zero-temperature value in various scenarios, including strong, weak, and marginal couplings. Subsequently, we investigate how the renormalized velocity affects charge carrier density and the resulting specific heat in doped graphene sheets. Finally, we explore the renormalization of the velocity along armchair and zigzag edges of doped graphene nanoribbons, demonstrating the interplay between Coulomb interaction and geometric constraints.

In our proposed system, MaskedSpeech, we develop a data-driven method to enhance the naturalness and emotional expression of speech synthesis. Unlike conventional approaches that rely on statistical models of probability, we use a masked language modeling technique to train a speech synthesis model. By masking random segments of input audio and training the model to predict these sections, we significantly improve the performance of the system, resulting in a 19% relative improvement in the MOS score and a 43% relative reduction in mean absolute error in arousal evaluation.

Building upon the NLS equation with an anharmonic oscillator, we investigate the presence of an external linear potential in both one-dimensional and two-dimensional NLS equations. One-dimensional periodic solutions and two-dimensional bounded solutions, in the form of an algebraic scar, are examined within this modified framework. By numerically inducing a small anharmonic disturbance in exactly solvable scenarios, such as the linear in-dimension and harmonic out-dimension, we study the impact of anharmonicity on these solutions. In one-dimensional systems, we find that anharmonicity leads to orbital instability in solitary waves and the generation of anharmonic edge waves in finite systems. In two-dimensional bounded domains, we observe anharmonicity causing the emergence of an algebraic scar pattern from anharmonically perturbed harmonic oscillator waves. These anharmonic effects result from anharmonically induced mode mixing and the excitation of anharmonic edge and scar states at the expense of harmonic interior modes.

Q-balls, a fascinating phenomenon in high-energy physics, offer valuable insights into the interplay between symmetry-stabilising fields and non-linear Goldstone boson interactions, particularly in complex potentials that involve multiple stable symmetries. Due to the complexity of these systems, incorporating Lorentzian constraints would likely complicate the problem even further. Nonetheless, we have observed in our previous study that the SU(2)xU(1) electroweak symmetry can give rise to multiple stable Q-ball Chandrasekhar-Friman limits, leading to the creation of multiple Q-ball species with different charges. These species can interact with each other in various ways, resulting in the possibility of one Q-ball overdensity being converted into another, and ultimately giving rise to the formation of cosmologically large Q-ball clusters with varying charges. Such phenomena have the potential to significantly impact gravitational wave patterns and affect particle colliders through the modification of Q-ball seeded inflationary models. To explore these theories further, we plan to develop a publically accessible, user-friendly tool that allows for the visualisation of our potential results, along with the corresponding theoretical frameworks.

We have developed a novel model of cyclic universe cosmology, which arises from the intersection of two cosmic principles: holographic dark energy and the de Sitter entropy formula. To prevent infinite cyclic reconnections, we have introduced a non-trivial cutoff based on the Olbert-Oliveros formulation, which significantly alters the periodicity of the universe. Our model demonstrates that the universe's cyclic nature can be linked to the existence of quasiperiodic structures like the Lévy fractal, giving a new, geometric explanation for the universe's cyclic behavior.

Given a graph G and a Galois field Fq, the qth power graph Gq is created by raising each edge of G to the power q. If L(G, x) represents the graph's L-function and L(Gq, x) for the graph Gq, then L(Gq, x) can be expressed as (1-x)L(G, x)/L(Sn, x), where Sn denotes the complete graph with n vertices. This relationship provides a way to compute the L-functions of Gq and its connected components using the L-functions of the original graphs G and F. This approach has already been established for quadratic and cubic power graphs. The current study delves deeper, exploring the L-functions of Gq for powers greater than 3. Specifically, it identifies the L-functions for Gq in instances where G is an n-cycle, a complete graph, a disjoint union of edges and trees, and certain non-trivial graphs with 12 vertices or less.

In this research, we explored the relationship between the additive Galois module structure of Q and a non-abelian finite base extension F of rational numbers, with the condition that F's ramification is wildly directed and it does not share a prime with six. Building on previously established theories by Kummer, Leopoldt, Grummitt, Padaik Kalis, and Clunie, we demonstrated that a freely generated condition is both necessary and sufficient for deriving a complete set of invariants within the Galois module structure of Q, with these invariants being computationally measurable through arithmetic CMJ invariants of F's rational base primes. Furthermore, our research provides the framework for a method to classify and generate all possible Galois module structures of Q, achieved by classifying and generating all possible strongly ramified, non-abelian, finite base extensions of the rational numbers, with a wildly directed and not sharing a prime with six condition.

The investigation at the Large Hadron Collider for a neutral long-lived particle, such as the stop $\tilde{g}$ generated through an R-parity violating process, is explored. This study examines how the decay length of the particle affects the suitability of certain search strategies at the collider. It is assumed that the top quark produced in the process has a significant branching ratio, with the decay chain top quark decaying to neutral mesons. A comprehensive analysis of detector simulation reveals that for a decay length of up to 10 millimeters, the stop is identified through the characteristics of top quarks. However, for larger decay lengths, the production of long-lived neutral systems leads to the detection of systematically longer decay lengths. A subsequent search strategy is developed to find such patterns, and with an integrated luminosity of 3 inverse abregees per deci-TeV of data, a discovery potential of 0.12 is found for a stop with a mass of 1.98 TeV and a decay length of 1 meter.

This study explores the concept of contextual coherence in relation to semantic change.
It first develops a computational model to measure contextual variance.
The researchers then conduct an experiment which reveals that increased contextual
variance masks semantic shifts, while a subsequent experiment identifies situations
where contextual coherence is either instrumental or a major obstacle to detecting
semantic changes in words. The paper also presents an experiment which demonstrates
that existing models based on supervised learning underestimate the degree of semantic
change occurring in words.

A new analysis of 1/T constraints on ultra-light particles, specifically axion-like particles and scalar fields, has been performed using existing dark matter experiments and radiofrequency cavity searches. These constraints, based on the behavior of particles in relation to de Broglie wavelength and Compton wavelength, are particularly relevant for ranges where conventional lorentzian approaches fail. As a result, the study provides fresh perspectives on ultra-light particles' role in dark matter composition, potentially allowing for the explanation of both primordial gravitational waves' anomalous phases and the cosmological lithium problem. Finally, the research sheds light on the potential for future experiments to uncover evidence of ultra-light particles in dark matter.

Understanding retinal development requires insight into the interactions between retinal cells as they migrate, multiply, and arrange themselves in an orderly manner. Due to the complex and dynamic nature of this process, as well as the large number of cells involved, it has been challenging to study retinal development in depth using conventional methods. In order to overcome these difficulties, we employed high-resolution, high-speed light sheet microscopy to capture and analyze ganglion cell nuclei migration across the mouse retina in vivo. Our study uses quantitative analysis and retinal cell fate mapping to examine the relationship between the distribution of nuclei and the patterns of cell fate across the retina. Our data reveal that the patterns of cell fate follow a spatial structure that is distinct from the patterns of nuclear migration, suggesting that these patterns may be influenced by different factors. Notably, we observed that the patterns of cell fate become more orderly as the retinal cells continue to develop, with a specific type of cell fate mapping the entire retinal surface. Our findings provide valuable visualizations of retinal development, offering a new perspective that can inform the study of vision disorders and eye system development.

Compressive sensing, an efficient image acquisition technique, can be vulnerable to ambiguities in matrix analysis. Recent studies suggest that a highly structured sensing matrix, built from a series of Fourier matrices, can lead to impractical resolution limits in image reconstruction. This note presents a simplified, generalized approach for generating comparable reconstruction performance with unstructured sensing matrices. By randomly sampling non-overlapping coherent sub-vectors, a mutually incoherent sensing matrix can be created, allowing for optimal reconstruction using the L1 minimization method. This technique is particularly useful for compressive sensing systems that require the implementation of structured masks.

Active systems at the edge of stability exhibit similar scaling to linearized hydrodynamics in dimensions four and above, but display distinct behavior in lower dimensions three and below, with additional steady-state modes affecting their scaling in these dimensions. These additional modes contribute to the scaling in dimensions three and above, but only influence the scaling in dimensions two and below, with their inclusion necessary to accurately describe the behavior of active systems near phase transitions.

Research institutions rely heavily on email communication and often share data with colleagues, clients, and government agencies, necessitating robust email security. A notable security vulnerability in research email networks has emerged in recent years - email-based money laundering - where criminals exploit compromised email accounts to steal funds. This study proposes an innovative approach to detecting such threats, combining machine learning with network analysis to identify suspicious financial transactions linked to research email accounts. Our model's initial phase uses email content and sender-receiver history to identify potential money laundering risks, followed by a second phase that incorporates network analysis to validate high-risk transactions. This hybrid approach was tested on a real-world dataset obtained from a Malaysian research university's email system, yielding a notable 90% accuracy rate in detecting email-based money laundering. This research offers an original solution to an existing gap in the literature and has practical implications for detecting email-based money laundering in research institutions.

In cuprates, combining theory and experiment suggests that an exceptional van Hove singularity causes the Lifshitz transition, occurring at the critical point where the Fermi surface changes from being hole-like to electron-like. This singularity makes itself known through an unusual magnetic susceptibility in the normal state, and is intimately connected with the anti-aliasing phenomenon that generates the kink in the electron dispersion near the critical point. Theoretical models that accurately depict this singularity, and the associated anti-aliasing and kink, must also capture the interrelated Lifshitz transitions, van Hove singularities, and magnetic susceptibility anomalies seen in cuprates. The problem is that current multi-orbital models have it backwards, with the magnetic susceptibility anomalies being the primary result of the van Hove singularity, rather than the other way around. The purpose of this paper is to outline an experimental case that must be met by any theoretical model of the cuprates: multi-orbital models specifically referring to d-band orbital van Hove singularities, and incorporating the anti-aliasing phenomenon and the kink in the electron dispersion, and and and and and and and and and and and and and and and and and and and and and and and and and and and and and and and and and and and and and and and and and and and and and and and and and and and and and and and and and and and and and and and and and and and and and and and and and

To investigate the Michel-Ellis effect, a highly efficient neutron detection system was developed, utilizing a specialized liquid scintillator containing Gadolinium chloride and enhanced by the addition of a plastic neutron converter. Studies were conducted with a 22Na source to analyze the detection efficiency of neutrons and scions, and a detailed comparison was made with existing research. The findings showed that incorporating Gadolinium into the liquid scintillator significantly increases the detection efficiency of neutrons by a factor of approximately 3.6, and that the addition of the plastic converter boosts this efficiency by a factor of about 3.8. With this optimized detection system, the production of positrons and neutrons from the decay of 22Na was measured at 83.78% and 5.52%, respectively, with an accuracy of about 0.01%.

This research paper supplements the studies of M. Masiello, G. Savarese, and P. Sweitzer on variational problems governed by a minimax rule, found in [1] and [2]. We specifically address and expand upon the results found in [1], which deals with the application of a minimax principle to a two-player game scenario described by a differential inclusion. Building upon the earlier work, we have derived new existence and uniqueness criteria for the solutions to these variational problems. These conditions are based on the minimax principle and are defined by the interplay between relaxed stability and asymptotic strong continuity properties. We have also established an expression for the minimal and maximal values of the solution set. Furthermore, we have obtained an existence and uniqueness theorem for the solutions to these variational problems under certain asymptotic strong continuity conditions, which does not rely on the relaxed stability property. This research was supported by the Italian National Group of Mathematical Physics and the Fondazione Angelo Raffaelli.

A thorough examination of the relationships among stars, systems, and planets within a cluster is a crucial aspect of the scientific potential of highly capable telescopes. Future instruments like the James Webb Telescope will allow the study of exoplanetary systems around hundreds of thousands of stars. To take full advantage of this data, researchers need simulations to accurately predict how planets form and change within these systems. By analyzing multiple factors, including the scattering of planets following the disruption of a stable system and the diverse range of planetary architectures that can emerge from similar initial conditions, a team has developed a protocol for comparing theoretical models to observational data. This approach prioritizes the complex relationships among stars, systems, and planets, allowing for a more nuanced understanding of how planetary properties emerge. The team applied this framework to a simulation of the TESS satellite's data, covering approximately 300,000 stars over a period of two years. The simulation included the creation of systems with up to seven planets within a cluster of 10,000 stars. To analyze these systems, the team divided the celestial bodies into categories based on their characteristics, such as habitable zones, terrestrial worlds, gas giants, and small bodies like dwarf planets and asteroids. By following the orbits of the planets within each system over time, the team could determine how many celestial bodies fell into each category. When comparing their results to a control group where the systems were not subject to disruptions, the team found that the cluster showed significantly more diverse planetary architectures, with a greater proportion

The rapid spread of ID card-based contactless payment systems necessitates efficient automated text extraction methods from IDs. Although Optical Character Recognition (OCR) technology has made significant progress, human-guided fine-tuning of OCR is often necessary, but labor-intensive. This paper introduces an innovative approach that combines OCR and Natural Language Processing (NLP) for accurate automated text extraction. Our proposed method utilizes a pre-trained OCR model and a language model, leverages the structural benefits of sequence-to-sequence models, and is demonstrated using Chinese ID cards as an example. Experimental results show that our approach achieves a high extraction accuracy of 96.5% without human intervention, outperforming the conventional OCR-based method with a margin of 8.4%.

The interplay between classical and quantum mechanics is a central theme in the study of driven systems in the quantum regime. Researchers in the field of nonlinear physics are particularly interested in coherent states, which serve as stable, observable bases for systems driven by forces with negative differential gain. This paper provides an overview of recent findings concerning the equilibration of coherent states in systems that exhibit chaos in both their classical and quantum manifestations, as well as a discussion on future research directions in this area.

Our team conducted a series of Hubble observations at ultraviolet wavelengths
around the Milky Way's central 0.5 parsecs, resulting in the discovery of seven
new UV sources, along with enhanced data on three existing ones. By cross-referencing
these findings with infrared and radio data, we classified these sources as
extreme scintillating X-ray binaries in the final stage of binary evolution. During
these observations, we also detected 21 new asteroids orbiting Sgr A*, along with
radial velocity curves that reveal five accelerated rotation curves, four
rotationally synchronized orbits, two possibilities for rotation or synchronization,
and one disputed case. The accelerated rotation of these asteroids offers valuable
insights into the formation of the Sgr A* system, and their orbits suggest the presence
of a planetary population that has contributed to the stabilization of the Milky Way's
central black hole over the past billion years.

Online forums enabling opinion expression on political topics allow users to engage with a wider audience, producing a record of discussions that can be analyzed to reveal community behavior and user interaction within those communities. By examining a dataset of opinions shared online, we can observe users joining communities based on their opinions, which facilitates the examination of community evolution. A mathematical approach, inspired by random community evolution models, is utilized to develop an analytical framework that accounts for the likelihood of users with similar opinions joining the same community, as well as the likelihood of community members sharing new opinions. This framework is applied to study the distribution of community sizes and the underlying parameters that govern community evolution, using methods to conduct approximate Bayesian inference. Through the analysis of Reddit discussion forums, we demonstrate the effectiveness of this framework in identifying community evolution patterns and the parameter that governs community size.

Let a subgroup G of differential operators act on the interior of a compact smooth surface S. Assuming the action is transitive and has no fixed points, we can find a fundamental domain for S consisting of finitely many regions with smooth boundaries. These boundaries are mapped to each other by the elements of G and can be shown to be non-retractable. Furthermore, if the surface S has no boundary, we can prove that the action of G on S is freely transitive and show it implies the analyticity of the surface S within a specific set of smooth surfaces.

A significant advancement has been made in understanding M-dwarf properties by combining thousands of precise stellar radii measurements with stellar evolution models. By establishing a direct relationship between mass and radius for these stars, it's now possible to accurately identify objects like planets, without needing detailed analysis of light curves. This breakthrough "M-dwarf zero-point calibration" can be utilized in missions like TESS, PLATO, and LUVOIR, especially when searching for exoplanets within the M-dwarf family. A comprehensive analysis of various factors influencing the measurement of M-dwarf masses, particularly the importance of spectroscopic analysis, follows the presentation of the new radius-mass relation. This study also outlines strategies for utilizing the established relation to derive more reliable masses for individual low-mass stars across upcoming exoplanet surveys.

Graphene patches can generate line waves in the microwave and optical regimes due to their unique edge properties. Recent studies have focused on applying these patches in sensing applications, and research is being conducted to understand how different designs influence line wave propagation. This paper investigates the theoretical foundation behind line wave propagation, providing an alternative explanation based on carrier density and velocity in the Dirac equation. An analytical formula is derived to calculate propagation velocity, showing that it is inversely proportional to the square of the spatial periodicity of the line wave. This relationship is validated through numerical simulations of graphene strips with varying widths. The findings of this study can be applied to improve sensing performance in Graphene by adjusting the periodicity of line waves.

Building on previous work by Dawen, Li, and Wang in 'Query Answering via Joint Sampling', we develop a comprehensive theory for evaluating the tractability of queries with self-joins in a broad database context. Our framework encompasses both probabilistic and traditional database scenarios, and we demonstrate that self-join queries can be computed efficiently if, and only if, they meet specific 'chainability' criteria with respect to a given set of functional dependencies. For the instance where functional dependencies form a cycle, we provide an adaptable parameterized algorithm for determining the tractability of self-join queries, and its corresponding complexity is explored under various conditions. Furthermore, we explore how our findings apply to both probabilistic and traditional databases, and establish connections with existing research on self-join queries, query answering, and database theory.

Determining whether a given set of polynomials represents a rational function whose points of continuity conjoin with given affine varieties within a specific Galois field is equivalent to a problem that has been previously unaddressed in the context of computational complexity theory. We demonstrate that this rational function reconstruction problem can, in fact, be solved using algorithms that are both efficient and deterministic, and this capability holds true regardless of the characteristics of the polynomials in question. The development of this solution relies heavily on the applications of a specific algorithm within the context of Gr\"obner bases, combined with various techniques related to the decomposition of polynomials, and the application of computational complexity-related principles, including the use of a Cyclotomic Field Generator that is based on a specific Cyclotomic Polynomial Generator previously described in the literature. The existing approach to this problem allows for the determination of the underlying rational function itself, rather than just its points of continuity, and this modification is achieved through an extension of a specific algorithm within the context of Gr\"obner bases, and the application of additional computational complexity-related principles. The existing approach to this problem also places the underlying Galois field within the context of a specific computational complexity class, and this capability is achieved through an extension of a specific algorithm within the context of Gr\"obner bases, combined with the application of additional computational complexity-related principles. Researchers from LHCb studied the $B^0$ and $B_s^0$ meson decays into $K^0_S K^0_S$ at the LHC using a data set of 3.0 inverse picobarns. They measured the differential branching fraction for both mesons, as well as the longitudinal polarization fraction for $B^0$ decays, finding significant results for both. The differential branching fraction for $B^0$ decays into $K^0_S K^0_S$ is $IB^0(K^0_S K^0_S)\times10^{-7}= 5.56\pm0.29\pm0.26$, with a longitudinal polarization fraction of $f_L=0.381\pm0.084\pm0.054$. For $B_s^0$ decays into $K^0_S K^0_S$, the differential branching fraction is $IB_s(K^0_S K^0_S)\times10^{-7}= 1.82\pm0.45\pm0.20$, with a longitudinal polarization fraction of $f_L=0.109\pm0.434\pm0.174$.

Machine learning techniques have recently been successfully integrated with reservoir computing to accurately model complex systems exhibiting multiple time scales and dynamic states. This study delves into the fundamental reasons behind the success of this approach and investigates the systems with periodic, quasi-periodic, and chaotic dynamics that reservoir computing can efficiently handle. We investigate the performance of the reservoir learning algorithm by evaluating its ability to replicate the time-dependent spectra of these systems at various time scales. Three distinct systems with periodic, quasi-periodic, and chaotic dynamics are used in this study. The results show that the reservoir learning algorithm can easily handle systems with periodic, quasi-periodic, and chaotic dynamics up to specific Schreiber plots' Lyapunov exponents values. These findings provide a practical performance benchmark for the reservoir learning algorithm and can aid in assessing its applicability to a given system.

A new bias-corrected estimator has been developed that extends the concept of bias-reduced surfing to handle situations with known or unknown forms of smoothness. This estimator is particularly designed for linear specifications where variables follow a specific pattern of smoothness and where the smoothing parameter goes to zero at a rate that varies depending on the specific form of smoothness present. A key feature of the proposed estimator is its ability to provide a bias-corrected estimate of the unknown parameter while taking into account the effects of data aggregation, thereby providing an efficient and direct way to incorporate considerations of smoothness. Theoretical properties of the estimator have been established, demonstrating consistency and asymptotic normality under specific conditions. A practical application of the proposed method is demonstrated through an empirical examination of the relationship between income and consumption, utilizing U.S. data from 1920 to 2015.

Optimal feedback control is a crucial component in control theory, and its computational approach typically involves complex numerical methods to determine reachable state sets within a given time frame. This paper presents an alternative way to calculate feedback control through a state feedback linearization approach, which provides a more manageable way to analyze the reachable state sets and their evolution over time. By applying a specific control strategy, the paper shows that the reachable state set around an initial state can be precisely determined and described as a union of affine spaces that intersect to form a robust transversal tube. This robust transversal tube structure provides a clear understanding of how the state set evolves and allows for the explicit computation of the largest time t at which the state set can be distinguished from the full state space. This computation is achieved by examining the local dynamics around the equilibrium point and is shown to be equivalent to solving a set of linear differential equations for a specific time t. Finally, the paper demonstrates its concepts by applying the feedback linearization approach to a mass-spring-damper system.

Following the success of frequency-domain processing in handling signal data, researchers have explored analogous transformations for spectra and images. Recent studies have demonstrated that applying the Fourier transform and utilizing frequency-domain representations significantly enhance neural network generalization, particularly for low-dimensional signal data. This paper builds upon and expands upon these findings by investigating the benefits of local-functional representations in both theoretical and practical aspects. Initially, the Fourier transform's uniqueness properties are leveraged to prove that multiple equivalent representations exist for any signal, implying that the Fourier transform is not a distinguishing feature of signals. Furthermore, the paper delves into specific examples featuring sinusoidal and B-spline signals to demonstrate alternative equivalent representations. In order to practically assess the generalization capabilities of frequency-domain representations, the author conducts various experiments utilizing neural networks across multiple data domains, including ensembles of quadratic curves, both in isolation and combined with signal data. The results show that generalization performance is consistently improved with frequency-domain representations, particularly for low-dimensional signals, and that multiple equivalent representations can lead to overfitting when using local functions with multiple degrees.

Human perceptions of living things fall along a continuum from non-living objects to animals, influenced by various factors such as visual appearance and interactive behavior with the environment. This study challenges the conventional assumption that this continuum can be broken down into distinct categories based on whether an object is man-made or natural. Instead, we explore the animacy continuum in its entirety through a series of experiments, discovering that categories are more fluid and universally the same across cultures. The findings reveal that the perception of living things is governed by two independent factors: how easily the object can be categorized visually and how the object interacts with its surroundings. The results also show that there are only three primary factors that govern the animacy continuum: motion, visual categorizability, and agency, with visual categorizability playing a more significant role than agency. The study further demonstrates that there is no need for sophisticated theories or models to recognize objects along the animacy continuum; a simple neural network is sufficient. The research includes an innovative method of collecting cross-cultural data through online experiments and an original dataset of animacy recognition trials. The study's discoveries and methods contribute to a revised framework for understanding the animacy continuum, with implications for improving computer vision models and developing more effective approaches to visual recognition tasks.

This study examines the distribution of zeros for automorphic L-functions within a specific region, potentially shedding light on the existence or non-existence of Landau-Siegel zeros. By analyzing a novel function derived from L-functions, specifically its zeros, we demonstrate the prevalence of a zero repulsion phenomenon, its magnitude, and consequences. These consequences imply the rarity of Landau-Siegel zeros and their extension to a broader class of L-functions, as well as the absence of multiple zero clusters for most automorphic L-functions. Our primary result is an extension of a previous finding by Bombieri, Conrey, and Perelli, with a more refined estimate of $\kappa \geq 5.53$. This estimate is obtained through the application of convolution methods and the introduction of a novel zero-counting formula.

This research expands the quantum relational Hoare logic we previously developed, 
allowing a more detailed examination of how a program's input relates to its output. 
We first demonstrate that adding this level of analysis, despite its increased 
complexity, still results in a logically decidible pre-condition-post-condition 
specification. 
We then show that existing quantum programs, including those using qregisters and 
pseudocode, can be re-expressed in this extended logic without altering the 
fundamental properties of which programs are valid. 
Furthermore, existing reachability algorithms for quantum programs can be adapted to 
operate within this extended logic, enabling the determination of whether a 
specific program state can be reached from an initial state without having to 
explicitly model the entire relational aspect of the program's input-output behavior. 
We outline the logical rules governing this extended quantum relational Hoare logic 
and prove that logically valid programs remain valid even with this additional 
relational analysis. 
We also present a practical example demonstrating how existing quantum programs 
can be safely re-expressed in this extended logic using qregisters and pseudocode. 
Our research provides a logical framework that can be applied to the specification 
and verification of quantum programs, enabling a more detailed examination of how 
a program's input relates to its output.

This study explores how super-spreader events impact infection transmission within confined spaces and contrasts their impact with standard epidemiological models. We develop a percolation theory-based epidemic model that accounts for the exponential growth of super-spreader infections, with parameters applicable to various environments. Our results reveal that enclosed settings can see a significant increase in infection transmission, with the R0 reproduction number exponentially rising to an infinite value. In contrast, standard epidemiological models with fixed R0 are less accurate in modeling super-spreader events. We demonstrate that a single super-spencer event can lead to widespread infections across entire subway systems, highlighting the critical importance of early intervention and targeted control measures in preventing the dissemination of super-spreader events.

A continuous group of operators on a Banach space is analyzed, along with its generated codiskiclicitiy property. The codiskiclicitiy property is reinterpreted in an invariant form, and then codiskiclicitiy is established as an essential property of the group operators. Additionally, the codiskiclicitiy property is linked to the continuity of the group operators' adjoints in an extended space.

Accurate information about a sunspot's magnetic field is crucial for understanding solar cycle behaviors. The Solar Optical Lever Arm (SOLA) technique effectively accounts for magnetic field properties on the solar surface. However, certain factors such as magnetic field concentrations within the sunspot and the extent of magnetic field coverage can either positively or negatively impact the accuracy of these assessments. A new approach utilizes the SOLA technique in conjunction with magnetic field potential reconstructions to create Vector Magnetic Field (VMF) maps. Notably, these reconstructions assume a linear relationship between the magnetic field strength and the potential, which may not hold in areas of high magnetic field concentrations. These limitations can result in inaccurate assessments of the magnetic field, even after applying the SOLA correction. A statistical analysis of the magnetic field concentrations within 69 large sunspots between 2004 and 2015 reveals the following key findings: - The magnetic field concentrations within sunspots adhere to a power-law distribution, with an index of 1.57. - The potential magnetic field energy exhibits greater concentrations than the linear magnetic field component. - The linear magnetic field component is overestimated, while the magnetic field energy is underestimated when utilizing the SOLA technique without adjustments. - The magnetic field energy assessments are more accurate when considering the magnetic field fill fraction. - The underestimation of the magnetic field energy when utilizing the SOLA technique without adjustments increases with more concentrated magnetic field areas. - The magnetic field fill fraction has a significant impact on the accuracy of

We examined the population of young star clusters in six late-type spiral galaxies, comparing their cluster populations to predictions from the Galactic Bulge's cluster population model. Observations from the Hubble Space Telescope led to the discovery of thousands of clusters in each galaxy, with ages ranging from 0.1 to above 10 billion years. By analyzing the density of clusters on galaxy surfaces, we found it increases with age, contradicting previous findings but aligning with predictions of the Galactic Bulge's cluster population model. The shape of the density histogram also changed from a Gaussian distribution for older clusters to a broader, more flat distribution for younger ones. The density of clusters around high surface brightness regions was higher than in low surface brightness areas. The location of these clusters followed the distribution of light across the galaxy's surface, with a slight concentration in central regions due to the mass concentration in these galaxies. The shape of the density function was consistent across all observed galaxies. By comparing the density of clusters and stars, we found the specific star formation rate in the galaxies' centers was higher than in outer regions. This led to an increased cluster formation rate in central regions. As a result, the surface density of new clusters in these regions was higher, explaining the higher cluster density in galaxy centers.

A new approach has been introduced for calculating the decay widths of particles in a finite volume, which addresses this issue through the use of sum rules. This strategy involves relating a decay width to a ratio of correlation functions in a specific channel. The approach has several advantages, including being lattice-notation independent and free from the contamination of low-lying states. Building on previous work, we have developed a framework that generalizes these concepts to decay processes involving multiple particles and both bosonic and fermionic degrees of freedom. The resulting formulae provide precise definitions for decay widths in a finite volume, which can be used as a basis for both lattice and field-theoretic calculations.

By integrating a novel type of layer into the neural network, the reliability of its Monte Carlo evaluations can be significantly enhanced for a broad class of problems defined by the theory of random Schr\"{o}dinger operators. This breakthrough is made possible by affinity coupling layers with complex coefficients, which are specifically tailored to amplify certain features important for the desired outcomes, thus efficiently isolating them during the Monte Carlo process. As a result, these modified neural networks excel in two key areas. Firstly, they produce highly accurate predictions in scenarios where the training data is significantly limited. Secondly, they significantly reduce the computational time required for the Monte Carlo simulations, allowing them to handle vast numbers of evaluations. The performance of these neural networks is so impressive because they can perfectly replicate the behavior of processes defined by the Schr\"{o}dinger equation, and as such, they can be an invaluable asset in the development of chemical compounds whose desired properties can be predicted using these processes.

This research investigates the number of integers, denoted as $y(x)$, that are $y$-friable up to $x$. The asymptotic distribution of the ratio of the logarithmic base change functions $\frac{\log x}{\log y}$ is analyzed and under the Riemann Hypothesis, a precise asymptotic formula for $y(x)$ is obtained, showing that it is approximately $\frac{x}{\log x}\frac{1}{\tau_2(\sqrt{\log x})}$, where $\tau_2(s)$ represents the second moment of the divisor function $\tau(s)$. Additionally, the investigation explores the distribution of $\frac{\log x}{\log y}$ and determines that when the Riemann Hypothesis is true, the distribution of $y(x)$ converges to a specific limit as $x$ becomes very large, allowing it to be approximated by a Poisson distribution with a rate of $\frac{x}{\log x}$ multiplied by the square of the Riemann zeta function's value at 2, i.e. $\frac{x \zeta^2(2)}{\log x}$.

This paper investigates how topological entropy is affected when a recognizable subshift is mapped through a recognizable and injective morphism, particularly in one-to-one correlations. We demonstrate that such a mapping's topological entropy is no greater than the pre-image's entropy, and if the mapping and subshift share a topologically free factor, the two entropies are equal. We also explore similar concepts with recognizable and bijective morphisms. For context, related results have been studied in non-finite state shift spaces using topological factors.

Contrastive learning helps next-generation language models excel in various tasks.
Despite its effectiveness, contrastive learning is often limited by the need for labeled data.
We present an innovative, unsupervised method called ReCross that employs a unique contrastive learning approach to extract rich semantic representations from unmarked text.
ReCross leverages the inherent structural connections within a dataset to learn highly generalizable and transferable sentence representations.
Our experiments demonstrate that ReCross levers up the performance of large language models in both unsupervised and few-shot settings, as seen in evaluations on the SuperGLUE and CommonsenseQA benchmarks.
For instance, our results show that a ReCross-transformer-base model achieves 80.8% unsupervised RoBERTa Baseline performance on the CommonsenseQA benchmark, outperforming the previous best score of 79.4%.

This research introduces a new mathematical function called m-ar-X and demonstrates its potential for use in high-dimensional data representation. By comparing it with widely accepted dimensionality reduction methods, the proposed function shows comparable performance in clustering and classification tasks, and has the benefit of being a more interpretable metric. A mathematical framework for m-ar-X is developed, and its underlying properties are identified, providing a foundation for future applications of this concept.

While Requirements Engineering (RE) plays a crucial role in the development of video games, the field remains under-theorized and lacks empirical data. Our research aims to bridge this knowledge gap by introducing a new empirical research approach specifically tailored for the gaming industry. We draw upon existing RE methodologies and gather data from various sources including the Internet, professional circles, and empirical project data. To validate our approach, we conducted a case study on the development of a puzzle game. We collected and analyzed requirements data, as well as development project information, to identify patterns and potential RE improvements. Our results yield valuable insights into requirements patterns, an RE methodology tailored for the gaming industry, and a reusable empirical research framework that can be applied to other video game development projects. By providing a framework for empirical RE research in the gaming industry, we invite the community to build upon and expand our work through further studies.

A prevalent challenge in machine learning research is selecting optimal model hyperparameters, a task complicated by strict data protection protocols which limit access to valuable private datasets. As a consequence, many potentially valuable models go underutilized due to difficulties in estimating their performance without access to the data they were trained on. In response to this problem, a new approach has been developed for approximately 10 popular optimization algorithms used in classification, regression, and support vector machines. This approach enables accurate hyperparameter selection without accessing the data, instead utilizing the model itself and a limited sample of the data (specifically labeled data). The new approach is compared to traditional methods like grid search and stochastic optimization on various datasets, and surprisingly found to be just as effective in some cases. The methodology underlying the new approach can also be interpreted as a form of regularized learning, and is found to result in meaningful improvements in some instances. Notably, this approach is applicable not just to linear models and support vector machines, but also to more complex models like neural networks and factorization machines.

Building upon previous work by Diaconis and Mitchell, who determined the number of spheres in a Coxeter system's subcomplex formed by a subset of generators, we expand upon this by investigating a similar subcomplex within a right angle. Specifically, for an irreducible Coxeter system with a subset of generators representing a right angle, we provide a non-trivial upper bound for the number of spheres formed within that subcomplex. This upper bound is shown to be minimally sufficient, as it is achieved or approached as the system's rank increases without bound. Additionally, we establish that this upper bound is at least twice the size of the system's generating set, and may be as small as three times that size.

The accurate assessment of source flux is crucial for astronomical detectors, which are often affected by correlated noise. Traditional methods that account for correlated read noise are based on the assumption that it only affects charge measurements. However, this may not always hold true, especially in modern detectors with complex noise patterns. A critical aspect is then identifying the relationship between noise and the non-linear device response, or lack thereof. For detectors like HRC on the AstroSat, with high energy resolution and spatial sensitivity, modeling the noise's impact on both energy and image analysis is essential. This paper presents the development of a noise model that accounts for the detector's response to X-rays, its probability distribution function, and its impact on charge distribution and image distortion. It also discusses the correlation between this noise model and traditional read noise models used in the past. This new noise model is being utilized in the development of source extraction algorithms that take into consideration the detector's noise characteristics.

The HERGS survey allows us to examine the chemistry of approximately 8000 stars in the Milky Way using spectroscopic analysis of far-ultraviolet spectra. By comparing observed spectra to predictions from the PEGASE model, we can identify any discrepancies in elemental abundances, including underabundances, in the data. Focusing on the 300 most chemically anomalous stars with unusual residual spectra, we grouped them by location within the galaxy. A comparison with standard galactic stellar samples revealed the distribution of the anomalous stars varies by region, with some areas exhibiting a higher proportion of stars with specific residual patterns. The discovery of numerous O-rich stars in the solar neighborhood, absent in outer regions, suggests these stars may be associated with a particular stellar population. The absence of O-rich stars among horizontal branch stars in the outer regions, coupled with their presence in the solar neighborhood, suggests a possible variation in the evolutionary paths of these stars, influenced by their initial metal content and location within the galaxy. This finding requires further exploration given the relatively small size of our sample.

In the complex spread of misinformation on social networks, previous research often focuses solely on existing peer literature, neglecting the significant role of initial sources and the underlying geography. Consequently, existing models fail to account for crucial factors such as the peer network's structural integrity and geographic proximity, which significantly affect the spread of rumors. This study addresses this limitation by developing a mathematical framework that models the peak and attenuation coefficients of rumors based on their precursor features and location. By applying multi-objective optimization, this framework allows us to identify optimal intervention strategies that maximize the peak of true information while minimizing the peak of false information, taking into consideration the underlying geography of the precursor sources. Numerical experiments validate the effectiveness of this approach, which can be employed to inform data collection efforts by pinpointing the most critical precursor sources for sampling.

Our study determines the distance to the Fornax cluster using the luminosity function of planetary nebulae and infers the cluster's mass within a specific radius. The analysis is based on data from 1995 to 2019 and includes 529 planetary nebulae. By comparing observed counts to model predictions at various distances, we determine the most likely value for the cluster's distance: approximately 12.76 kiloparsecs, with a margin of error of about 0.16 kiloparsecs. This measurement allows us to calculate the cluster's mass within a radius of 10 degrees: approximately 8.3 billion times the mass of our sun, with a margin of error of about 1.1 billion times the mass of our sun.

StreamSQL, a cutting-edge data processing language, enables fast in-memory aggregation on large-scale datasets. Its compilation into low-level bytecodes requires numerical libraries with highly optimized routines. StreamSQL's inbuilt numerical library, NumLib, is notable for its automated generation, creating binary code from a high-level specification at runtime. LifeStream is an advanced version of NumLib, capable of executing complex instructions simultaneously. In extensive testing, LifeStream's performance exceeded that of hand-optimized numerical libraries for popular datasets, including real-world applications like Twitter traffic and web search data. LifeStream successfully executed 109 different queries on a single core within a second, demonstrating its performance potential. LifeStream is particularly effective at handling large datasets in science and engineering, leveraging SIMD operations to achieve speeds 60-130 times faster than the existing NumLib library.

This study explores the concept of Bertrand curves in specific contexts, namely Euclidean space, where it's shown that given one curve, there is a unique second curve that maintains a constant distance, unless the original curve is straight.
