by leveraging modern multi-core hardware. Its success relies heavily on 
optimizing memory usage, as memory-intensive graph applications often have 
large in-memory datasets. To improve memory efficiency, the GP2 developers 
introduced a new data structure called BigArray, which can store massive 
amounts of data across multiple JVM arrays. However, the existing BigArray 
implementation, although better than the previous one, still has room for 
improvement. The GP2 team has optimized BigArray further by minimizing 
memory usage and improving performance, by reducing the memory overhead of 
each element by a factor of four, and achieving a significant increase in 
array operations per second. The optimized BigArray results in a notable 
reduction in memory usage and improved performance for graph programs. The 
new memory management capabilities enabled by BigArray make it possible to 
load larger datasets into memory. The most significant example is the 
TraversedSubgraphs program, which now requires 11 times less memory to run, 
and has also experienced a substantial boost in performance, with memory 
footprint no longer a key performance indicator in this case. The GP2 team 
has been able to load and process 1.3 trillion graph edges, achieving a 
new record for in-memory graph processing. The optimized BigArray has 
been successfully integrated into the TPC-H and TraversedSubgraphs programs, 
resulting

This paper introduces a novel, multi-task deep learning framework that efficiently handles both supervised and unsupervised feature extraction tasks. Our proposed method leverages a unique adaptation of the cycle-consistent deep unsupervised pre-training technique and incorporates a pair of discriminative modules, enabled by access to labeled data, for a semi-supervised modification. This enhanced framework not only facilitates unsupervised pre-training but also refines the learned features using limited labeled data, thereby amplifying the effectiveness of the features extracted. Our experimental evaluations on three diverse image datasets ($$CIFAR-10$$, $$CIFAR-100$$, and $$STL-10$$) demonstrate the advantages of our proposed method over existing techniques in both supervised and semi-supervised learning scenarios.

Building on earlier work by Cublayer and Giaculli, we present an infinite series of graph sequences, denoted as $G_{4t}$, along with their corresponding automorphism groups $\Pi_{4t}$. These graphs $G_{4t}$ feature 4t edges and a connected component structure that mimics the configuration seen in the Myshkin graph, which has a renowned automorphism group isomorphic to the free group $F_{3t}$. In contrast, the automorphism groups of our constructed graphs $G_{4t}$ are free groups of rank 2, thus providing an infinite family of examples where the graph structure contrasts with that of the Myshkin graph while its automorphism group also diverges from $F_{3t}$.

This research introduces the Group Lasso algorithm for selecting relevant variables from a dataset consisting of continuous or categorical information. The proposed method aims to reduce variables affecting an outcome variable, while maintaining the ability to distinguish between different categories of the remaining variables, the algorithm utilizes a Group Lasso technique to achieve this goal. We provide a comprehensive guide to implementing the algorithm, along with a set of flexible tools that can be employed with various R packages, specifically the 'ggplot2' and 'pheatmap' packages for data visualization. To validate the effectiveness of the algorithm, we created a simulation environment and applied it to real-world datasets, including those from the fields of life and medical sciences.

Deep neural network models pre-trained on knowledge graphs, particularly those utilizing triples, have shown significant gains in question-answering tasks when fine-tuned on natural language understanding benchmarks. Despite the intuitive appeal of this success, a surprising finding has been observed: models pre-trained on knowledge graphs consistently outperform their text-trained counterparts in many cases. This study aims to further explore this phenomenon by comparing models pre-trained on knowledge graphs and text using various evaluation methods, examining the origins of this performance difference and potential limitations of models pre-trained on knowledge graphs. Our primary observation indicates that models pre-trained on knowledge graphs exhibit over-reliance on graph structure and may struggle with semantic reasoning tasks. Moreover, we observed that models pre-trained on knowledge graphs can excel in question-answering tasks due to the inherent relevance of their Triples, but may fall behind in cases where the knowledge graph contains less relevant information. Additionally, we discovered that models pre-trained on knowledge graphs can exhibit performance boost when applied to tasks related to the training data, but may decline on tasks outside the knowledge graph. Overall, our results provide a more comprehensive understanding of models pre-trained on knowledge graphs and their capabilities, as well as limitations, in comparison to models pre-trained on text.

This article examines how classical partial differential equation models narrow to their corresponding kernel-based nonlocal counterparts as the kernel's extent decreases, with the exception of the Keller-Segel model which terminates in a singular limit. We explore both continuous and stochastic frameworks, investigating both first-order diffusion models and second-order elliptic/parabolic equations. We demonstrate the nonlocal-to-local framework's broad applicability across various PDE models, including mean-field interactions, phase transitions, and stochastic systems. We also derive a new approach for applying spectral theory to kernel-based equations by leveraging the relationship between the kernel and its nonlocal limit. This new perspective provides a spectral dynamic approach for analyzing the equilibria and stability of solutions within the nonlocal setting.

Wireless sensors, specifically IMUs and UWB devices, can facilitate image capture and subsequent processing for panoramic image creation. Our research introduces a novel, real-time approach for panoramic image generation utilizing these sensors. Unlike conventional methods heavily reliant on computational power, our process leverages optimization techniques and gradient-based updates powered by sensor data, allowing for more efficient and accurate results. A 2D representation of key frames, guided by the 3D spatial information provided by the sensors, is created through a Murry-Van-Loi operator-inspired process. Our system is tested using a mobile device, with results showing its capability for real-time panoramic image creation.

This preprint outlines the decomposition of a specific set of degenerate Eisenstein series under right translations, in the context of GL(3, A). The investigation relies on Weyl group cosets for its analytical tools. The studied degenerate Eisenstein series belong to the space of automorphic forms generated from an irreducible, nontemporary representation of a cover of GL(3, A). The study also utilizes completed cohomological forms for a specific, nontrivial central orbit. The results provide a novel application of the Weyl group cosets and an extension of prior research on degenerate Eisenstein series for GL(2, A).

All-around movement issues characterize Parkinson's Disease, an central nervous system disorder due to the degeneration of motor neurons, and it has no cure yet. Understanding the brain-hardware linking system is vital to effectively modeling its functioning and developing efficient prosthetic control methods. Advances in computational models, driven by cutting-edge machine learning techniques and rich neurophysiological data, have enhanced knowledge and paved the way for novel testing frameworks. By applying evolutionary optimization to a relatively simple model of the basal ganglia, we successfully demonstrated the potential of machine learning to overcome significant challenges in Parkinson's research. Specifically, we utilized evolutionary reinforcement learning to train a computational model to accurately mimic the natural brain signals associated with voluntary movements. Our results showed that the model could be trained to produce similar brain patterns when performing tasks, despite being trained on synthetic anisotropic Gaussian nosise, and could learn optimal brain-hardware parameter settings that result in smooth motor function and minimal oscillatory movements. This study's outcomes have significant implications for the development of effective brain-computer interfaces in the treatment of Parkinson's Disease.

This research introduces a novel algorithm for accurately rendering line joins in digital fonts, specifically targeting the imperfect results produced by the standard font rendering engines. The primary defect in commercially available fonts is the poorly rendered "L" shape, which has only a single pixel connection, leading to a broken appearance. To address this, a new line-merging technique has been developed, capable of splitting one of the "L" shape's endpoints into three, producing a more aesthetically pleasing curved connection. Building upon this technique, an edge-splitting module was created to effectively handle various line combinations, resulting in the OpenRTRenderingEngine. The proposed system successfully re-renders font glyphs, producing high-quality output from a customized font library, Fetta. The improved results, obtained through the inclusion of edge-splitting capabilities, are being openly shared via an online demonstration, along with the NISTSpecialFonts library, which comprises 100 fonts.

Using observations from Gemini, GMOS, GMOSif, FIREBOS, and VLT/MX, we have discovered evidence for AGN-driven outflow systems in six low-luminosity type-1 AGNs in the center of merging galaxies at moderate redshift. These outflows, which are interacting with both the merging galaxies' molecular gas and the newly formed stellar disks following the mergers, have features such as broad, multi-velocity-width H-alpha lines, outlying star clusters, and outflowing CO gas. The outflows were activated around the time of the galaxy mergers, around 200-500 million years ago, and have had a lasting impact on the galaxies' evolution. The outflows are also contributing to the growth of supermassive black holes, which are a key aspect of galaxy-sMBH co-evolution. The discovery of outflow systems influenced by AGN in merging galaxies provides valuable insights into the role of mergers in galaxy-sMBH co-evolution and the potential for heavy element circulation.

In this research, a novel universal smooth rational Hermite interpolant (USRHI) was developed for a broad category of functions, based on a general framework that includes the classical Gaussian, Hardy and Bi-Hamilton operators, and it has been demonstrated that this interpolant preserves the characteristics of convexity and monotonicity. Building on the USRHI framework, a specific rational Hermite interpolant was created using the generalized compactly supported RBFs and it was shown that this interpolant exhibits the same convexity and monotonicity properties. Notably, this RBF is distinct from the commonly used power function RBFs such as the hypersingular operator, power function RBF and their combinations, and it offers several advantages over them, particularly in terms of stability, efficiency in computation and ease of implementation. Several numerical examples have been presented to illustrate the performance of this new RBF-based interpolant in comparison with the classical ones.

Deep Convolutional Neural Networks (DCNNs) have reached peak performance in image classification tasks, but they have one major limitation - they are not transparent in their decision-making process. One way to enhance the understanding of these networks and prevent them from being easily manipulated, is to implement robust input features that remain consistent across various transformations of the input image. For instance, rather than using entire images as input, they can be broken down into smaller regions, such as super-pixels, that remain intact even after the application of image processing techniques like cropping, rotation, and flipping. This paper introduces a new data generation method that uses delimiting masks to create multiple robust input features from a single image, with the goal of reducing the overfitting of trained models and increasing their generalization ability. Through the use of Delaunay triangulation, each super-pixel can be divided into two distinct input features: a central region and its surrounding area. By generating multiple robust input features from a single image, such as by applying different Delaunay triangulation, we can increase the diversity of training datasets. We evaluated the effectiveness of this new data generation method on two popular benchmark datasets, CIFAR-10 and Stanford Cars dataset, and observed a notable improvement in the generalization performance of pre-trained ResNet-18 networks.

A recent Deep-Paced Convolution Recurrent Network (DPCRN) model has been proposed to achieve high-quality speech enhancement using a dual-path mechanism. This model leverages a combination of wide and narrow convolutional filters in the frequency and time domains respectively. Despite its success, the underlying physics behind DPCRN's performance is not yet fully understood. Our in-depth analysis, supported by both numerical and visual evidence, reveals that DPCRN can be viewed as a complex speech enhancement method operating within the time-frequency domain. In this domain, DPCRN's dual-path structure allows it to tap into two beneficial properties: the elimination of unwanted harmonics and the removal of unwanted time-frequency sparsity. These benefits are achieved as a result of the wide filter's ability to eliminate the DPCRN's tendency to introduce time-frequency sparsity and the narrow filter's capacity to eliminate the DPCRN's tendency to introduce unwanted harmonics. Our analysis also highlights that deep neural networks (DNNs) are capable of achieving speech enhancement similar to DPCRN when utilizing multi-layer dual-path structures. However, this comes at a significant cost including increased computational requirements and noise vulnerability. On the other hand, our results show that wide deep neural networks (DNNs) outperform their narrow counterparts in terms of speech reconstruction and robustness. In order to further enhance DPCRN, future research should focus on developing objective functions sensitive to the time-frequency domain in order to provide better optimization tools.

Evaluating the distribution of ratios from turn-around radii can help break the cosmological dark sector degeneracy when combined with constraints from power spectrum measurements. Our analysis used a suite of exact $N$-body simulations based on varying dark matter and dark energy parameters. These parameters included different scalar perturbation theories with separate and intertwined $w$ and $w'$ values, as well as the impact of massive neutrinos. The study focused on the statistical properties of the turn-around radii by comparing the ratios of their distribution to theoretical model predictions. These ratios were calculated using the relative differences in radii for specific overdensity thresholds and the apparent break in the distribution at certain points. Our analysis found that the turn-around radii ratios exhibit distinct differences in the presence of neutrino free fields, resulting from the altered formation of structures within a specific radii range. When incorporating the effects of neutrino fields, additional variations in the turn-around radii ratios resulted from the increased deformation of the power spectrum. Consequently, the combination of neutrino-based constraints with those derived from the turn-around radii ratios' analysis allows for a significant reduction in the parameter space of the dark sector, ultimately narrowing the acceptable range for $w$ and thus $\Omega_\nu$.

A new two-fluid model is proposed to explain the behavior of turbulent layers in fluids undergoing Rayleigh-Bénard convection. By assuming a distinct kinematic fluid for temperature fluctuations, separate equations for momentum and heat are derived, resulting in a self-sustaining mechanism for turbulent down-drafts that can overcome the Marangui-Presse hypothesis limitations. This model successfully predicts the observed heat flux plateau and critical Rayleigh number relationships for both water and mercury within the asymptotic convection regime. Additionally, it reveals that turbulent layer universality may stem from fluid properties influencing interface fluctuations rather than being an inherent property of the fluid itself.

When a cavity interacts with an uncorrelated atom, the entanglement between the cavity and the atom develops due to collapsed states, leading to shifts in the optical properties. However, these properties can be restored by choosing appropriate laser frequencies. Our research reveals that the cavity's interaction with multiple, uncorrelated atoms results in two opposing factors: (1) the entanglement between atoms, which could potentially lead to multipartite entanglement, and (2) the influence of the cavity on the atoms' optical properties, which could result in optical parametric amplification or absorption. By selecting suitable frequencies, we demonstrate that the cavity's influence on the atoms' optical properties can be overridden, enabling the creation of optical Schrodinger cat states between two atoms, even when the cavity is initially unentangled with the atoms. Conditions for the required optical control are also identified.

The CMS experiment at the CERN LHC upgraded its silicon pixel detector as part of the Total Budget Upgrade, with the aim of maintaining its track and vertexing capabilities for the 2016 delivered luminosity spectrum and beyond. To achieve this, six additional pixel layers were installed around the beam pipe, with the closest being 12.10 cm from the beam line. The upgraded detector features 96 Tesla Pixels per square centimeter, with an overall coverage of 4 by 4 centimeters, and an expected in-flight straigh-track efficiency of 99.937%. Through in-flight straight track reconstruction with cosmic muons, beam tests, and final production acceptance verification, the upgraded detector met its efficiency goals. The installation of the upgraded detector took place in August 2016, about one month before the 2016 long shutdown.

The quantum chromodynamics (QCD) sector is explored through the lens of its adhesive sphere spectrum, which has been extensively studied across various lattice QCD simulations, by examining the contributions of instantons, and within the context of an SU(2) gauge theory with a fundamental fermion. The study employs lattice Monte Carlo simulations to determine the glueball spectrum and investigate the effects of a non-zero quark mass on this spectrum. Additionally, the lattice Monte Carlo simulations are complemented by an SU(2) gauge theory with a fundamental fermion, which enables the examination of how instantons influence the glueball spectrum. A comparison is conducted across these scenarios to gain insight into the nature of the adhesive sphere spectrum and its relationship with the quantum chromodynamics theory.

This project combines Natural Language Processing and Deep Learning techniques to analyze public sentiment towards the COVID-19 pandemic on social media. We leveraged a vast dataset of tweets containing opinions about pandemic-related topics, extracting relevant information using BERT-based embeddings. Subsequently, we built two distinct sentiment analysis models employing Long Short-Term Memory networks and Convolutional Neural Networks. These models were deployed on the FST-COVID dataset, yielding superior results with an accuracy of over 90%. Additionally, we conducted an in-depth comparison between the two classification approaches, demonstrating that the LSTM model outperformed the CNN model in terms of F1-score, accuracy, and robustness.

Investigating the non-linear Yang-Mills charge parameter's effect, we find it influences the shadow radius and thermal profile of black holes, indicating a connection between this parameter and the Hawking temperature or surface gravity. This investigation is executed across distinct spacetime settings, including the Einstein-Yang-Mills system, Einstein-Yang-Mills-dilaton system, and Einstein-Yang-Mills-axion-dilaton system. Our findings demonstrate that the non-linear Yang-Mills charge parameter plays a crucial role in determining the black hole shadow's size and near-horizon thermal distribution. Consequently, this parameter could be concretely inferred through astronomical observations of black hole shadows coupled with their temperatures, thereby providing a distinct method for verifying theory of gravity and deformed gauge theory dynamics.

The study offers a comprehensive description of the interplay between nonclassical phenomena and optical systems, building on previous work that showed the vast array of optical system configurations leading to distinct, entanglement-rich states. Here, an extensive set of such systems is mathematically modeled to demonstrate the diverse range of entanglement present within their optical projections, with specific examples including the double-slit system, Mach-Zehnder interferometer, coherent Jaynes-Cummings interaction, trimer system consisting of three cavities, and the linear array of N cavities. A thorough analysis of the phase space of these systems in their optical representation highlights the distinct areas where entanglement is present, showing how it alters the classical optical field distribution in certain areas while maintaining it in others. Furthermore, a classification of the distinct modes of entanglement is achieved by analyzing the symmetries unique to each system.

In data-driven dialogue systems, an approach known as dialog state tracking models has shown significant performance, but it is hindered by the requirement for vast amounts of perfectly labeled data. Recent research has explored the use of role specifications and partial labels to reduce the necessary data quantity. Despite advancements, previous methods primarily relied on the assumption that role specifications and partial labels are error-free. Realistically, these labels are prone to mistakes, and they pose a risk to the accuracy of the model. This study addresses this issue by presenting a model that learns from role specifications and partially labeled data, including mistakes, to predict complete and accurate labels. This model takes into consideration the quality of the labels, and it is formulated as an iterative process of label refinement. Experimental results on the DialogStateTracking dataset demonstrate the effectiveness of this model in producing more accurate labels compared to existing methods.

This research develops an integrated approach to prescribe multiple management strategies for the prevention and control of diseases in crop production, specifically focused on mitigating the risks of aphid-borne viruses in strawberries. The approach incorporates decision analysis to evaluate and compare various management options, given uncertainty in their effectiveness and costs, as well as stochastic changes in weather conditions and pest populations over time. A dynamic and adaptive management simulation was used to generate data on the expected outcomes of different management strategies, which were then applied to a decision analysis framework to determine the most cost-effective approach. The study used a case study of a strawberry crop in California, considering management actions like crop scheduling, sanitation, and chemical applications, as well as weather and biological factors like temperature, the presence of aphids and natural enemies, and the spread of the virus, to simulate and evaluate their impact on the crop's yield, quality, and profit over time. The results showed that managing the crop to avoid peak aphid populations, controlling the virus's spread, and adapting to changing weather and pest conditions were key to maximizing profit, and provided a framework for decision analysis that could be applied to other crop diseases affected by multiple biological factors.

Immersive video viewing is becoming increasingly popular due to advancing VR and AR technologies. As users watch immersive videos on mobile devices, a critical issue arises: predicting user viewing behavior. This task is crucial for reducing data transmission costs and enhancing viewer experience. Current deep learning models, although accurate, require massive data and are difficult to apply to real-world applications because of their slow training speed. Additionally, they fail to consider crucial factors affecting viewer behavior, such as video content semantics, making them less suitable for complex immersive video scenarios. To address these challenges, this work introduces a novel, efficient deep learning model that excels in viewing direction prediction while minimizing data requirements and training time. To prepare data for training, this model is paired with an innovative video annotation tool that leverages subtitles for accurate semantic object detection. As a significant aspect of this research, video subtitles are analyzed to demonstrate their inherent value in providing precise object labels. The proposed method's superiority over baseline models is proven through rigorous testing on two diverse, real-world datasets, resulting in significant improvements in viewing direction prediction accuracy, with an average gain of 14.7%.

By developing a suitable entanglement purification operator (EPO) network, we've successfully generalized the EPO framework to approximate bulk thermal states and time-evolved states from a given initial state in an open quantum system. This generalized EPO approach can efficiently produce approximate periodic unitary operators (PEPOs) with a specific bond dimension, showing that the required bond dimension scales quadratically with system size for approximating thermal states and time-evolved systems, in contrast to linear scaling for isolated systems. Our work provides the EPO framework's application to PEPOs and demonstrates that this method is a versatile tool for approximating complex many-body dynamics in quantum systems.

This lecture will build upon previous discussions regarding Taylor-based analysis and its applications in understanding decoupling properties, specifically within the context of canonical surfaces. We intend to demonstrate how certain Taylor series methods can be combined with the geometry of canonical surfaces to gain insights into the decay of Fourier coefficients and its relationship with almost orthogonality properties.

This paper establishes relationships between anisotropic capacity, Poincar\'e inequalities, and cylindrical John-Nash ellipsoids. Specifically, we demonstrate that the anisotropic capacity $K_p$ is equivalent to the $p$-th power of the volume of the John-Nash ellipsoid that minimizes the product with the determinant of its diagonal, and also shows connection to both the strongest possible Poincar\'e inequality and the largest possible cylindrical John-Nash ellipsoid in the space of ellipsoids with the same total trace.

A space-based experiment designed to measure the equivalence principle with high accuracy detects unintended spikes known as glitches in its data. These events occur frequently, around 150 times per second, and are caused by various internal phenomena. However, they also contribute a significant spurious acceleration signal, needed to be quantified and removed from at least one data set essential to this research. A statistical technique was employed to identify and eliminate glitches from the data, resulting in an acceleration measurement with an error margin of 1.5 x 10^-9 times the standard deviation, making it suitable for testing the equivalence principle with a discrepancy margin of 0.007 times the standard deviation.

Our research focuses on the motion of a specific class of active dimers that exhibit asymmetry in activity and force generation when interacting with the surrounding liquid. We have developed a theoretical model describing their dynamics, and through linearization and fluctuation analysis, we have derived an equation that predicts the dimer's motion and is directly translatable to its equivalent in a macroscopic device, such as a wheel. By examining the dimensionality of the surrounding environment, we have investigated how water's flow and confinement affect the dimer's movement, and have identified distinct regimes governed by hydrodynamic forces, surface tension, and steric constraints. Notably, we have found that dimers exhibit Brownian motion characteristic of one-dimensional random walks in both two and three-dimensional fluid environments.

We have derived two mathematical proofs to classify the k-strong shortest path union cover problem as NP-complete and show it has no approximate polynomial-time solution for fixed k greater than 1. A heuristic 2-approximation algorithm exists for general k, but we've developed a polynomial-time solution when k is fixed at 1, essentially solving the single-source shortest path cover problem. This solution is also applicable to the k-strongest path union cover problem. We've also discovered that covering all k-strongest paths in a graph is NP-complete and has no approximate polynomial-time solution, but a heuristic 2-approximation algorithm exists for fixed k.

The infrared renormalons in the structure function $F_2(x,Q^2)$ at the Jost function approach were calculated in a previous study, and it was found that the O($1/N_c$) terms in the instanton liquid model (ILM) match the expected renormalon pattern. However, the size of the renormalon-dominated contribution in the ILM does not fit the assumed two-loop uncertainty criterion in the lattice QCD parameterization of $F_2(x,Q^2)$. Instead, the ILM's renormalon-dominated term accounts for nearly the entire two-loop uncertainty in the structure function $xF_3(x,Q^2)$ as determined from neutron scattering data. As a result, the lattice QCD parameterization needs to be resolved into its renormalon components to accurately assess its systematic uncertainty in accordance with the Konishi anomaly approach.

Recently, Li and Zhang proved that a fern of degree $p$ is almost surely recurrent for $p\in (0,2)$ and Li and Zhang also showed transience for $p\in (2, \infty)$. This paper extends those results, finding the critical value $p_c$ where the fern changes from transience to recurrence, and also shows that a specific type of fern with variable edge weights also exhibits transient behavior. This finding narrows the possible structures of trees that have a transition from transience to recurrence, and it is speculated that any tree with a finite degree greater than 2 would also have a transition from transience to recurrence. This paper also analyzes the frog model on a specific type of tree that changes from transience to recurrence at a certain critical value $p_c$, and it is found that $p_c$ is the same as the fern that changes from transience to recurrence at the same $p_c$. This paper also provides an explicit formula to calculate the cover time of the fern when the degree $p$ is greater than 2.

In this research, the intricate spectral characteristics resulting from magneto-optical effects in a specific type of photonic crystals were investigated using a theoretical approach that incorporates advanced numerical simulations. The study examined a unique structure where a metal film, featuring surface plasmons with unusual behavior, is combined with a periodic array of apertures that give rise to Rayleigh anomalies after light transmission. The proposed structure exhibits unique features when light interacts with a nearby magnetic material, and the predicted spectral patterns were verified through numerical simulations. The findings showed that the interference between surface plasmons and Rayleigh anomalies, as well as magnetic materials, leads to the creation of magnetic mid-iron resonance and a hypernormous redshift, both of which are observable in the proposed design. The proposed structure and its associated effects also provide a foundation for developing novel magneto-optical devices, such as surface plasmon-based light emitters and switches, which can operate efficiently across the visible spectrum.

In knowledge distillation, a novel approach called black-box knowledge distillation allows a model without access to the knowledge source's parameters to transfer knowledge. I propose a new, fully black-box knowledge distillation approach called DB3, where a model without access to the knowledge source's parameters is trained to accurately classify a labeled dataset. Unlike traditional knowledge distillation, DB3 relies on the knowledge source's ability to correctly classify a randomly generated unlabelled dataset. DB3 outperforms knowledge distillation based on input salience, gradient matching, and temperature scaling. Experimental results demonstrate that DB3 can effectively reduce the parameter count of ResNets, MobileNets, and Tranformer models, while maintaining comparable performance on multiple image classification datasets.

Initially reported measurements of the branching fractions were updated by LHCb using a combined dataset of 3.0 fb^-1 of data.  LHCb evaluated the decay mode of $\Omega_b^0 \to K^0 \omega$ with an estimated branching fraction and single photon spectrum, also reassessing the decay mode $\Omega_b^0 \to K^0 \pi^+ \pi^- \pi^-$ to better understand its symmetry when considering charge conjugation.  LHCb obtained an updated estimation of the $\Omega_b^0$ mass using all available information, specifically the $\Omega_b^0 \to J/\psi \Omega$ decays which provided a more precise measurement of 6054.2 MeV/c^2, along with evidence of the $\Omega_b^{-2S}$ meson around an expected mass of 10355 MeV.

Let $\mathfrak{g}$ be a semisimple Lie algebra over the complex numbers, and let $V$ be a multiplicity-free $\mathfrak{g}$-module. Assuming $\text{Char}(\mathbb{C}) = 0$, we provide a detailed description of the lattice of submodules for any finite-dimensional $\mathfrak{g}$-module $V$, by establishing a one-to-one correspondence between its composition factors and irreducible $\mathfrak{g}$-modules. This correspondence is constructed using the highest weight vectors for the module $V$ and its submodules, and a similar approach has previously been employed for block-diagonalizable representations of the algebra of differential operators on flag varieties, with a similar method also used for calculating the lattice of submodules for certain highest weight modules for simple Lie algebras.

This paper explores the Strong Geodetic Recognition problem, which asks whether a given vertex subset in a graph contains a strong geodetic cover that coincides with the original subset. We have analyzed this problem for various graph types, specifically focusing on directed graphs. We have discovered explicit solutions or theoretical limits for certain types of strongly connected graphs, such as tournaments, circulants, and their combinations, while also finding general approaches for other graph types.

The main bottleneck of imitation learning is the high cost of labeling data. To overcome this limitation, we investigate whether few expert demonstrations can train a highly accurate policy across a broad range of tasks. Specifically, we explore the hypothesis that natural non-expert online data can be used in conjunction with limited expert off-policy data to achieve this goal. We introduce the TRAIL algorithm, which learns a policy that generalizes well to new tasks with minimal expert input. TRAIL first uses a general-purpose algorithm to train a policy using a wide range of tasks and diverse online data. It then identifies tasks that require expert guidance by measuring the gap in action probabilities between the general policy and actual online behavior. The identified tasks are then fine-tuned using the expert off-policy data, and the algorithm is incrementally updated to reduce the action probability gap. We provide theoretical guarantees for the generalization of the learned policy and demonstrate its effectiveness through a range of experiments on various datasets, including both simulated and real-world scenarios.

By learning from multiple agents with different levels of proficiency in a single shared environment, we've developed a novel framework called Co-Imitation Learning. This approach allows a less skilled agent to mimic the abilities of more capable peers, essentially eliminating the need for costly expert demonstrations. We've applied our framework to the challenging task of transfer learning in the complex Atari game Ms. Pac-Man, and achieved impressive results by leveraging the knowledge of high-scoring human players in a virtual environment populated by robotic agents. Our experiments show that Co-Imitation Learning outperforms both reinforcement learning and a state-of-the-art imitation learning method using expert demonstrations in Ms. Pac-Man.

The problem of a sequential decoder erring due to insufficient information being sent about a source that is known to be conditionally correlated is examined. The issue of how to properly determine the amount of data to transmit, taking into consideration a polarized cutoff rate as a suboptimal bias, is investigated for a binary memoryless source. The impact of using this biased cutoff rate on the probability of a sequential decoder making an error is quantified in terms of the probability of the corresponding binary erasure channel making an error, which can be evaluated using the polarized behavior of polar codes. Specifically, it is shown that using this biased cutoff rate results in the decoder erring with a probability that is at least twice as high as the optimal bias, which is achieved through the application of a threshold-based strategy to the source's conditional correlation structure. The accuracy of this comparison is ensured by constructing a sequence of binary memoryless sources with varying degrees of conditional correlation, which are distinguishable by any sequence-decodable testing scheme with a probability that is asymptotically high for large code lengths.

Previous studies have shown that reinforcement learning can significantly improve machine translation. However, the current approach, using a dense action space, has major limitations. We challenge this status quo and present a novel, compact action space based on the underlying latent factors of the encoder outputs. By reducing the action space density, we observe improved translation quality and model robustness across multiple evaluation metrics. Our results demonstrate that a subtle increase in action space compactness leads to a substantial gain in performance, and this optimization has a tangible impact on translation quality, surpassing the previous state-of-the-art baseline. Furthermore, our model exhibits enhanced translation diversity and fewer errors in unsupervised machine translation.

Accurate robotic sensor pose estimation is crucial for various applications including those in medical research and robotics. This study aims to enhance the robustness of end-effector pose estimation using machine learning by incorporating 3D visual data from a depth camera, specifically obtained with the Microsoft Kinect. A previous research demonstrated that adding depth data to RGB images improves pose estimation accuracy using a traditional optimization approach. This work builds upon that finding and compares three supervised learning methods--decision trees, neural networks, and random forests--to explore their ability to learn from both RGB and depth data for pose estimation. The results show that a combination of RGB and depth data yields better performance than using each image type individually and outperforms the traditional optimization approach. The study further investigates the impact of calibration on the performance and finds that adding depth data to RGB images significantly enhances pose estimation accuracy, especially in cases with poor initial conditions.

Continuous retracts and closed maps that reverse order play a crucial role in the study of Quasi-Frechet spaces (QFS-spaces). These retracts and maps are essential tools for achieving high degrees of generality in the classification of Quasi-Frechet spaces. Our research expands upon the current understanding of QFS-spaces by demonstrating that they are equivalent to defining a quasi-Frechet filter space for any topological space. This new definition is more comprehensive, yet it still maintains the same level of generality as previous concepts of quasi-Frechet spaces. Our study of QFS-spaces is accompanied by the development of several specific examples, including the reals equipped with an irregular topology, which do not fit into the categories of Frechet or Hursch spaces. Our findings also establish connections between quasi-Frechet spaces and continuous retracts within T3 spaces. We show that such retracts always induce quasi-Frechet filter spaces and that the resulting spaces are themselves quasi-Frechet spaces. This research is an extension of earlier findings presented in the authors' earlier publication.

Online media can foster political polarization, but its root causes remain poorly understood beyond surface-level factors such as social network dynamics and online news sites' perspectives. To address this knowledge gap, we have been studying the underlying mechanisms of political polarization through the lens of Web browsing habits. Specifically, we have been analyzing the spread of partisan online content based on users' browsing activities and observed a striking phenomenon - certain communities consistently prefer the same types of information over others, even when preferring different types of information is mathematically more likely. To study this phenomenon further, we developed an agent-based model that mimics Web browsing habits and assessed its effectiveness through analytical and simulation-based techniques. The results showed that the model not only accurately replicated the observed distribution of online engagement but also exhibited similar characteristics, such as community-level preferences and the divergence of opinions within these communities. Furthermore, we applied this model to analyze various aspects of online polarization in the United States, including how preferences are formed, opinions diverge, and online engagement varies depending on the topic and community in question.

The Thompson group V is one of the earliest discovered finitely generated amenable groups, and it has a renowned word problem that has been investigated extensively. By building upon the connection between the word problem of a group and a specific class of languages, it has been proven that the word problem for V is equivalent to a deterministic context-free language that does not accept all context-free words. This equivalence serves as the basis for the subsequent conclusion in this paper, which reveals that such a language indeed exists and can be generated through a context-free grammar while being distinguishable by a pushdown automaton.

Quantum information theory provides an interesting framework for studying the interplay between an open system and its environment. This study demonstrates that bidirectional information exchange can occur between an open system and its surroundings by leveraging quantum correlations known as quantum mutual information. This phenomenon is made possible by the non-conservation of information in the quantum world, allowing for the flow of information in both directions. An example involving an interacting particle and its environment, along with the discussion of a proposed experiment using trapped ions, is used to illustrate this concept. These scenarios highlight the potential for both the initial and the final states of the system to be either entangled or steerable. Consequently, this could provide the basis for the development of novel quantum protocols that leverage the non-linear interaction between a system and its environment.

This paper presents the results of a study on biharmonic recurrent operators for hypersurfaces within the Euclidean space of higher dimensions. Initially, the paper defines a new type of operator, \phi, which satisfies specific conditions for both the biharmonic operator \Delta^2 and the conformal operator C on a hypersurface. It is demonstrated that, on a higher-dimensional Euclidean space, any non-constant, biharmonic, recurrent operator \phi encompasses a significant portion of the hypersurface and, under specific conditions, can be expressed in terms of an harmonic operator. Furthermore, the paper establishes a novel condition for a biharmonic hypersurface to be minimal in the Euclidean space, expanding upon the previously established condition of W.Y. Chen and N. Kamada.

In this research, we provide a characterization for the (p/q)d-dimensional Diophantine sets that are recognizable by a regular expression in base p, building on a previous finding that these sets can be defined using a system of inequalities over a rational number set that is recognizable in base p. This characterization leads to an proof that the set recognizable by a finite automaton in base p is equal to the set that can be defined using a system of inequalities over a rational number set that is recognizable in base p, which further implies that the (p/q)d-dimensional Diophantine sets that are recognizable in base p are countably generated in the context of any rational number q and any positive integer d.

A new variant of the anomalous U(1)$_A$ extension of the standard model, dubbed $a_u$MSM, is presented, where the U(1)$_A$ symmetry is broken at the TeV scale while maintaining the stability of the electroweak vacuum and addressing the naturalness of the strong CP problem. The $a_u$MSM model involves three additional scalar fields with zero isospin and mass differences of the order of 10^{-3} eV, related to the axion mass, within the capability of IR sensitivity to differentiate it from other scenarios, offering a novel solution to the hierarchy of the quark mass scales. The $a_u$MSM is distinguishable from other scenarios by the anomalous Z$\rightarrow$4$\gamma$ and K$\bar{K}$ decays at the intensity frontiers of the ILC and NA62, offering a chance to uncover the fundamental origin of the quark mass hierarchy.

This paper introduces the LAMOST time-domain survey binary catalog, which contains 4761 candidate binary systems extracted from LAMOST's time-domain survey using imaging data from the ATLAS and ATLAS-1m telescopes.  By comparing the light curves of these LAMOST targets and detecting irregularities, we were able to identify 4761 candidate binary systems spanning 0.01 days to 1000 days in orbital period, along with luminosity classes from 0.1 to 10.  A random forest algorithm was used to eliminate 13494 probable variables not included in the catalog by analyzing their likelihood in each class.  Among the remaining candidates, there are 7831 detached, 2783 over-contact, and 247 semi-detached binary systems awaiting spectroscopic confirmation.  We expect to verify a significant number of these variables through spectroscopic observations, and many of these binary systems will be suitable for gravitational wave detection by third-generation gravitational wave detectors.  In addition, many of these variables exhibit unusual light curves that could be caused by the interaction between stars and extreme compact objects such as black holes or neutron stars.

In the context of image segmentation, the incorporation of Edge-Gated CNNs (EG-CNNs) has offered promising breakthroughs for Deep Neural Networks. This study delves deeper into the EG-CNN mechanism and undertakes a complementary exploration to uncover the underlying reasons for its success. Through systematic modifications to the EG-CNN architecture and rigorous testing on three diverse image segmentation benchmarks, we seek to isolate and examine the individual contributions of key components. Our results demonstrate that each aspect of the EG-CNN, including the Edge-Gated module and the integration with the base network, significantly impacts performance. By providing Edge-Gated networks as an alternative to standard network ensembles, our findings offer practitioners a more nuanced understanding of EG-CNNs and suggest they may be a valuable addition to the toolkit for image segmentation.

This study examines the concurrency properties of four widely used NoSQL key-value stores and distributed multi-version concurrency control systems under transient errors and node failures. We tested HAZELCAST, HBASE, MONGODBDISTRIBUTED, and CASSANDRA by simulating concurrent reads and writes, as well as client connections to random nodes, and found that CASSANDRA follows prefix consistency while HAZELCAST, HBASE, and MONGODBDISTRIBUTED satisfy snapshot isolation; WIREDTIGER, REPLICASET, and SHARDEDCLUSTER in MongoDB implement variants of snapshot isolation. We discovered that HBASE and CASSANDRA ensure atomicity even in the presence of node failures and transient errors, whereas HAZELCAST and MONGODBDISTRIBUTED may experience losses of updates under certain failure conditions; all systems experienced data loss in some scenario of concurrent writes.

Taking $T_n(\xi)$ as the sum of all $e$-positively modified chromatic symmetric functions of Dyck paths of size $n$, our main goal is to provide a complete breakdown of $T_n(\xi)$ into its individual $e$-positive components, referred to as $e$-alternating symmetric functions, when $n$ is two or greater. Building upon this decomposition, we establish a relationship between $T_n(\xi)$ and the sum of all $e$-alternating modified chromatic symmetric functions of Dyck paths of size $n$, and we demonstrate that this sum equals $\xi_{2n}$, the highest degree monomial in the ring $\ZZ[e,\xi]$. Furthermore, we use this relationship to derive a novel expression for $\xi_{2n}$ in the context of $\ZZ[e,\xi]$, and we are also able to express the $k$-th elementary symmetric function in this ring as the sum of all $e$-alternating modified chromatic symmetric functions of Dyck paths whose size $n$ satisfies $n\geq 2k$.

This paper introduces the notion of hindsight summarization in machine learning, 
where past events are condensed into more compact, relevant summaries for optimal 
outcomes. We argue that summarization can enhance learning by reducing prediction 
errors from past experiences. Building on the foundation of optimal policies learned 
through reinforcement learning, we develop a goal-directed summarization framework 
that ensures attended experiences are optimized. We further introduce the concept 
of offline hindsight summarization, enabling the selection of most relevant past 
interactions when learning from static datasets. Through numerical evaluations, 
our proposed methods prove capable of efficiently selecting the most informative 
past experiences, either online or from static datasets, with significantly 
improved performance compared to random selection.

The development of high-quality datasets is crucial for training and evaluating models in medical image analysis.  However, certain implicit biases present in these datasets can compromise the generalizability of models and lead to unfair predictions.  This study investigates the existence of biases in the ACDC dataset used for cardiac multi-class segmentation.  Firstly, a quantitative metric was established to measure the similarity between shapes of different ethnic groups based on 3D mesh analysis.  Then, a random forest classifier was used to detect shape-based stereotypes, and the feature importance was used to identify the influence of categories on this bias.  Secondly, a comparison with the 2018 Cardiac Challenge dataset revealed differences in the distribution of patients with African origins.  Lastly, the results of this study suggest that the implicit biases found in the training dataset can influence the performance of models on unseen data, and that certain techniques such as data augmentation may not be sufficient to rectify this issue.  To address this problem, new strategies are needed that focus on reducing the influence of category labels during training, such as constraint learning.  Future work should involve validating the findings of this study across additional datasets and developing robust methods to detect and quantify the biases present in medical image datasets.

We studied Ising spins interacting on a network composed of interconnected triangles, arranging these interactions in a specific pattern to replicate equivalent interactions found in certain hexagonal arrangements. Our main goal was to examine the magnetic properties resulting from these interactions by simulating and numerically solving the Kuramoto model, a suitable simplification for this scenario. Our findings show that the spins follow a unique hysteresis loop shape, characterized by asymmetric loops, and we observed how varying interaction strength and temperature affected this behavior, ultimately leading to an equilibrium magnetic state in our system.

New insights into the distribution of energy sources that allow small bodies to escape solar gravitation's influence are gained by studying the behavior of dust particles ejected from the Jupiter family comet C/2013 A1 (Siding Spring) as it passed close to Mars in 2014. Although most particles disintegrated or were captured by the sun due to the intense light scattering, a significant number survived this ordeal and were tracked as they journeyed towards the inner solar system. Analyzing post-perihelion paths of this comet's particles allows scientists to identify the energy inputs that enabled some particles to overcome solar gravitation's grip at very close distances to the sun. These inner solar system regions feature extremely high levels of solar radiation but very little else, so the survival of post-perihelion paths at very small distances implies that photoelectric forces become significantly more powerful than previously estimated, typically surpassing 10 mN by the time they reach 0.1 AU. Comparing these findings to computational models and previous studies of dust particle trajectories in our solar system reveals that more energy is required to navigate the sun successfully, especially in the most inhospitable regions near the sun, and that this energy can be attributed to the collisional dissipation of electric field components rather than other mechanisms like cometary activity.

This paper introduces a cutting-edge, multi-language and corpus emotion recognition network. It's the first known model to achieve emotion recognition on multiple languages, rather than being confined to a single language. The proposed framework leverages a unique, proposed dataset called MOSE, which comprises data from four languages - Chinese, English, Japanese, and Korean. This dataset allows the model to achieve remarkable performance on three of these languages, outshining existing benchmarks. Notably, the model exhibits notable adaptability on data with labels removed, demonstrating a capacity to learn from data without relying on pre-trained models, and showcasing an impressive ability to generalize across languages. It's worth mentioning that previous studies on multi-language emotion recognition were limited to comparisons between languages like English and Chinese, due to the lack of a comprehensive dataset. This model's performance on MOSE sets a new standard, and it has the added benefit of recognizing emotions in text form. This is particularly significant because existing models and techniques tend to focus solely on audio-based emotion recognition. The proposed model's performance on MOSE, which includes a vast collection of drama movies and TV shows, solidifies its position as a pioneering, multi-language emotion recognition system.

By utilizing high-pressure synchrotron radiation, researchers have discovered a novel Bi$_5$FeTi$_3$O$_{15}$ phase that emerges at extremely high pressures, exceeding 10 GPa. To understand this phase, scientists have employed density functional theory under pressure up to 12 GPa, revealing that the structure comprises an Aua$-3m$ polar aerogel lattice. This study also examines the phase's stability, lattice parameters, and dielectric behavior under increasing pressure. An anomalous pressure increase in the dielectric constant of Bi$_5$FeTi$_3$O$_{15}$ is found to correlate with the onset of this new phase, indicating potential for improved ferroelectric properties. To facilitate device fabrication, the phase can be stabilized at lower pressures through the application of lateral electrical fields. By manipulating these fields, multiple structural phases may be achieved in this material system.

In control theory, errors in systems dynamics and control objectives can significantly impact the performance of optimal control problems. A localized error bound comparison method an alternative to comparing error bounds globally, can improve the evaluation of discrete control performance when systems evolve continuously. However, this method has limitations in assessing the accuracy of optimal discrete control trajectories when they significantly diverge from their continuous counterparts. A new method, developed using localized contrastive learning, can enhance the accuracy of discrete trajectories by exploiting differences in data representing systems in motion. It leverages the fact that the physical constraints of a system limit the diversity of its underlying dynamics. Therefore, learning a representation where similar underlying dynamics have similar representations, and learning a contrastive loss for distinct underlying dynamics, enables accurate discrete trajectories even in the absence of a continuous reference. Notably, this method outperforms existing techniques on challenging optimal control problems requiring precise timing and trajectory control.

A nonlinear acoustics model is developed for a strong shock wave in a non-ideal gas, allowing for dissipation represented by a general form of Rayleigh's resistance to shear. The model is validated through comparisons with both direct numerical simulations and various other theories, particularly those of Landau and Lions for non-linear and linearised regimes respectively. A new mechanism of instability, characterised by an $O(1)$ perturbation scale, is discovered and analysed through a nonlinear asymptotic technique called multiple scales. A specific equation governs the behaviour of the shock wave's core in the presence of a certain range of adiabatic powers. An existence and uniqueness theorem for the linearised equations under certain boundary conditions is established. A new regime, previously unknown, is identified by comparing the model with the linearised equations. The model's parameters determine the prevalence of various regimes. A map of the adiabatic power space, classified into distinct regimes based on the model's parameters, is created and different regime classifications are defined in terms of their dynamical systems properties. A map of the dissipation parameter space is created, classifying it into stable and unstable categories depending on its value's sign. The model's parameter values are determined and classified into different categories based on the behavior of solutions for the linearised equations. Decay rate parametrization plays a crucial role in determining Nu-Clustering-Tagging Variables (NCTVs). While the Caprini-Lellouch-Neubert framework has been widely adopted, alternative approaches like the Caprini-Lellouch-Neubert and Boyd-Grinstein-Lebed schemes also exist. We examine the relationship between these frameworks and NCTVs, focusing on $B\to K\pi$ decays. Our findings reveal that the Boyd-Grinstein-Lebed scheme directly connects to the Nu-Cluster-Tagging Variables, providing a clear and intuitive understanding of their physical significance. Within this paper, we also derive the decay rate parametrization for $B\to K\pi$ in the Boyd-Grinstein-Lebed scheme and establish a connection to the corresponding axio-pion observables.

We demonstrate that one-dimensional supersymmetric non-singular potentials, which allow scalar field coexistence, are analogous to the standard harmonic oscillator potential, using the Heisenberg Weyl algebra, specifically in the $N=1$ and $N=2$ scenarios. This equivalence reveals a direct connection between the number operator and the supercharge in the 1D SUSY QM context. This relationship's exploration leads to the identification of short-range confining potentials in $N=2$ scenario that are linked to the Bessel oscillator potential. We also derive the associated ground state energies for these linked potentials. Furthermore, we extend this framework to its two-dimensional counterpart for both the harmonic oscillator and Bessel oscillator in both spinless and supersymmetric scenarios.

This subject revolves around the complex dynamics of the H\'enon map, a simple quadratic planar system renowned for its chaotic behavior. We begin by analyzing the stability of its invariant manifolds, demonstrating that the Lyapunov exponents used to measure stability are highly sensitive to initial conditions. This sensitivity is utilized to develop a method for locating and distinguishing between the system's positive and negative Lyapunov exponents. This approach enables the creation of a global map that identifies the spectrum of Lyapunov exponents across the entire phase plane. This global map exhibits distinct isolated regions corresponding to distinct values of the exponent ratio, ultimately leading to an understanding of the systems' dynamical transitions between coherent rotation, coherent oscillation, coherent formation, and coherent scattering.

Researchers investigated an asymmetric Superconducting Quantum Interference Device with coupled Josephson junctions, considering the impact of phase-locked oscillations on its switching current. Unlike a standalone junction, whose switching current is directly proportional to the asymmetry, the effect of phase locking is found to be inversely connected to it. A formula derived from simulations provides the switching current in terms of locked modes and phase-locked oscillation frequencies. The study also reveals that the locking current, which determines how much current is needed to lock specific modes, is inversely related to the asymmetry in the symmetric limit but instead correlates with it in the asymmetric case, albeit in an opposing manner. These findings are significant in the development of highly accurate voltage standards based on SQUIDs with coupled Josephson junctions.

We've developed a quantum field theory model that includes a non-abelian aether term for Yang-Mills theory in $(1+1)$-dimension. This model exhibits a non-abelian Stefan-Boltzmann law, and our calculations indicate that the non-abelian aether term results in an alteration of the expected $\frac{1}{12}$ power law variation, instead yielding $\frac{1}{4}\left(1-\frac{1}{N}\right)$ for large gauge groups. Likewise, the non-abelian aether term leads to an infinite correction to the Casimir energy, with the value depending on the coupling constant and the rank of the gauge group, thereby diverging as the rank increases, thus diverging the Casimir energy from the expected linear relationship with the coupling constant, with the proportionality constant being $\frac{\pi^2 N}{24}$.

This paper presents two original numerical integration formulas that can be used to model the interaction between buy and sell orders on a limit order book. By approximating the expected value of a random variable that results from the interaction between orders, the introduced formulas can determine the cumulative distribution function of that variable. One of the formulas is particularly suited for calculating the expected value before a specific event occurs, such as a hedging event, and can be computed more efficiently than a common alternative method based on Monte Carlo simulation. The paper also verifies the accuracy and efficiency of the new formulas through numerical experiments.

This paper builds on existing research that uses variational methods to analyze certain integral functionals for vector fields, subject to specific linear differential constraints, within a broader framework. Specifically, we expand on previous findings that utilized these methods to investigate the regularity of potential theory and its connection to the Fourier transform, by further incorporating the use of the Riesz transform.

This study presents TDGS, a new tidal feature dataset consisting of 1031 galaxies without spiral disks, observed in the optical spectrum and spanning a wide range of stellar masses from 9.0 to 10.5. The research focuses on tidal tails within this sample and reveals how tidal features due to major mergers are distributed among low-mass galaxies. A notable asymmetry is observed in the distribution of tidal tails according to galaxy mass: tidal tails are significantly more prevalent in more massive galaxies. The percentage of galaxies exhibiting tidal features that are not mergers also increases with mass. A key concept in research on social inequality is opportunity allocation, which refers to how resources or positions are distributed among individuals in a population. This distribution can either reinforce past inequalities or provide new chances for individuals from disadvantaged backgrounds. The question of how opportunity allocation affects the intergenerational transmission of socioeconomic status is the focus of this study. We have developed a mathematical model that simulates the passage of time and includes two types of processes: random events with distinct probabilities that either help or hinder an individual's progress, and a mechanism for allocating new opportunities that allows for either a fair or biased selection process. We have analyzed the conditions under which the socioeconomic status of previous generations influences the current and future generations and have investigated the impact of opportunity allocation on the inequality gap. Our findings are confirmed by means of algorithms in the context of discrete time increments.

This paper provides an in-depth analysis of complex photon systems, specifically CPA and NLO-based systems, using an integrated approach that combines theoretical laser modeling and rigorous numerical methods. The difficulty lies in accurately capturing the intricate interactions between intense lasers, NLO materials, and CPA systems. Our approach leverages AdK's description of CPA systems and Type-I NLO interactions to set up a complete CPA/NLO system model. We employ a beam-envelop e method, an integral equation method, and a Lagrange-Galerkin technique to solve the resulting equations efficiently. Our method is flexible, allowing for various physical descriptions and numerical solutions. As a demonstration, we apply this framework to model a CPA system comprising an amplifier, a laser, and a beta-Barium Borate crystal, showing good agreement with existing Monte Carlo simulations. This work lays the groundwork for further investigation of CPA/NLO systems, enabling faster and more accurate simulations of multiple-beam, multi-physics scenarios, and facilitating the development of novel CPA/NLO applications.

For $p \neq 2$, the linear operators that map the unit ball of $\ell_p$ isometrically onto a subspace with a dimension less than $p$ are non-existent, demonstrating that the property of isometric dimension reduction does not apply in this case. Additionally, this concept's failure is utilized to provide counterexamples in the context of vector-valued sequences, the absence of certain operator families, and the non-existence of specific subspaces with specific properties.

Precise measurements of beam-beam interactions in particle colliders are crucial for understanding long-range multiparticle beam behavior. To facilitate this, we propose a method for accurately measuring the orbits of interacting beams using interferometry techniques. Given the sensitivity of this method, we expect it to directly reveal the magnitude of beam-beam effects at a rate of up to several hundred per hour for each intersection point combination. Furthermore, we anticipate this method to be applicable in the context of future high-luminosity colliders.

A new approach to distributed optimization, involving a network of agents that can communicate with each other, is being developed. The goal is to have a fast and efficient way to minimize a cumulative function, where each agent has access to a part of the function. The challenge is that the communication between agents is not perfect, as some agents may send false information on purpose, and there are also physical limitations to consider. It is assumed that a fixed number of the agents are trustworthy and willing to cooperate, but the rest are either uncooperative or malicious. This paper develops a new method that uses a combination of gradient updates and communication between the cooperative agents, with the option to adjust parameters to balance the trade-off between reducing the total loss and resisting the negative impact of uncooperative agents. It is proven that the proposed method leads to the creation of a set that includes the optimal solution, and that the set can be made as small as desired. This result provides a way to balance the benefits of adding more cooperative agents, through increased communication, and shows that the total loss can be minimized up to a certain point, despite the influence of uncooperative agents.

The Science Simulation Service (S3) has been successfully utilized by the Cherenkov Telescope Array (cta) consortium for instrumental systematic effects simulation. By leveraging this experience, we propose adapting the S3 framework to expedite the development of next-generation CTA instruments through in-depth simulation of instrumental systematic effects across various simulation scenarios.

This study compares the performance of various sequence-to-tree transducers, including linearized models, with the goal of word ordering, using the tree linearization task as a reference, and investigates the advantages of a newly proposed linearized model known as Linearized BART. Our findings demonstrate that linearized models excel in word ordering, with Linearized BART exhibiting the highest accuracy, while the existing linearized model named Linearized Transition-Based Neural Parser also achieved impressive results. Notably, Linearized BART outperformed all other sequence-to-tree transducer models, including neural network models, with an overall F-score of 89.2%, outperforming the best sequence-to-tree transducer model by a significant margin of 5.6%. Our experiments involving augmented data and parsing errors revealed that Linearized BART's enhanced performance can be attributed to its transition-based architecture. Additionally, Linearized BART's components, including the encoder and decoder, were found to be highly effective, with the encoder playing a crucial role in word ordering.

In the current digital age, the dissemination of deepfakes through various social media platforms poses a significant threat to public safety and credibility. Given the endless possibilities of deceptive videos, they can be easily created and distributed, and as a result, automated multi-platform deepfake detection is now a pressing necessity. Unlike existing single-platform classification systems, our proposed framework, DCNet, is capable of identifying deepfakes across diverse domains, leveraging domain-aware modules and cross-stitch connections that facilitate the exchange of features between domains. Through the incorporation of these connections, our network can effectively exploit domain-specific information, prioritize feature importance, and prevent the leakage of sensitive domain information. As a result, Deepfake samples from diverse domains can be distinguished more accurately by the network. Furthermore, our experimental findings demonstrate substantial enhancements in robustness and performance when utilizing the proposed multi-domain aware modules and cross-stitch connections, outperforming the current state-of-the-art models by over 10% on the cross-domain deepfake detection benchmark.

A new class of non-regular low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes, derived from random graph ensembles with specified degree distributions, has been investigated for its error-correcting performance under erasures rather than channel noise. The focus of the study was on LDPC codes with negative degree-degree correlations, which require an alternative decoding approach since the standard sparse message-passing algorithm is guaranteed to converge only within limited erasure probabilities when degree correlations are non-negative. Numerical simulations compared the performance of negative degree-degree correlation LDPC codes under erasures during the decoding process and found that an increased initial erasure probability allowed for correct code decoding, with a maximum threshold depending on the specific degree distributions used. As a theoretical basis, an upper-bound expression was derived to quantify the maximum initial erasure threshold probability, which represents the highest erasure probability that can be tolerated during the decoding process for LDPC codes with negative degree-degree correlations. The proposed bound includes well-known cases and provides a quantitative measure of the improved robustness of negative degree-degree correlation LDPC codes under erasures during decoding.

In a weak decoy state quantum key distribution system using a vacuum and a single photon, the attacker can exploit this vulnerability without detection, intercepting the weak decoy state and adding a multi-photon, which reduces the phase error rate, ultimately allowing him to generate the key. We derive an error threshold for the weak decoy state, which must be below a certain minimum in order for the system to remain secure. This minimum is expressed in terms of the gain for the vacuum and weak decoy states, and must be less than a specific fraction of the former. We also establish a threshold for the ratio of the coding efficiency of the weak decoy state to that of the signal state, which must be below a certain minimum in order for the system to remain secure. This minimum is expressed in terms of the gain for the vacuum and weak decoy states, and must be greater than a specific fraction of the former. We demonstrate the applicability of these findings through simulation of the system using the Finer and Sasaki decoy state gain formula.

This paper addresses the challenge of minimizing energy consumption in edge computing systems through load scheduling. We model the problem by assigning tasks to reduce energy costs at the edge, taking into consideration processing requirements and load coexistence at each location. A proposed method involving approximate optimization and a local refinement process aims to provide efficient and effective solutions. Additionally, we explore the application of reconfiguring edge computing nodes to minimize energy consumption in an overlay network. Our results show that the proposed techniques lead to substantial reductions in energy consumption, with the scheduling method achieving particular notable gains.

This paper expands on previously established results by Widman and Shoen, which defined an angle function in certain types of spaces and used it to determine conditions for conformal embeddability. We have expanded the concept of angle function to apply in a broader context - in complete, non-compact Riemannian spaces with specific boundary characteristics. Our research provides a more comprehensive approach to previously solved problems in this area, while also offering a more flexible framework for studying conformal embeddability in complex spaces. Building on earlier work, we have established and proven several theorems and lemmas regarding the properties and applications of this expanded angle function function. Our results include demonstrating its relationship with the K\"ahler metric, establishing its maximum value under certain conditions, and developing an expression for its Laplacian in the presence of certain symmetry conditions. We have also discovered a method to modify the angle function through the use of a non-increasing function, which has significant implications for solving the conformally invariant Dirichlet problem in these complex spaces.

Leopoldson and Yui address the issue of non-uniqueness for local Zoll orbits by establishing an uncountable number of distinct isomorphism classes of orders in number fields that exhibit a particular geometric property. Furthermore, they derive a general inequality that expresses this property in terms of Gelfand diagrams, and this inequality serves as a precursor to previous inequalities of Bass, Grayson, and Rainbird. The context in which these inequalities hold has been broadened to include cases where the field is a finite extension of Q_w, and it is implied that a significant proportion of locally Zoll lattices arise from orders in such fields.

This work examines how pressure affects the breakdown of a nitrogen jet flowing over a flat surface, as it undergoes a sudden transition from a stable laminar flow to a highly turbulent state. High-resolution particle imaging and phase Doppler anemometry were used to investigate and compare the flow patterns at two different pressure conditions, 0.1 MPa and 0.5 MPa, where the latter simulates pressure found in most flight environments. At the higher pressure, the break-down of the jet occurs more rapidly, both in terms of distance from the nozzle and time, and the development of turbulent behavior is accelerated by the increased pressure. As a result, a ring-shaped vortex forms more quickly at higher pressures, and the flow becomes more turbulent, with larger Reynolds numbers and increased shear stress, despite the decrease in temperature and the increase in density. The data also reveal enhanced mass flux and flow acceleration in the turbulent region at higher pressures, both in terms of magnitude and thickness, and the shape of the vortex ring.
