Eventually, the agents send their findings to the central computer, and a more efficient optimization method is used to update the learning model. Because of the vast difference in processing capabilities between the central computer and the agents, what appears as a vast distance in steps (e.g., $10^{18}$) is actually a very small distance in pseudorandom walks. As a result, the central computer can easily determine with high probability that new misclassified specimens are located near existing data in the classifier network. This allows the central computer to decide which agents to direct towards which newly collected data in order to expand the classifier network. This method can handle thousands of agent connections with minimal communication requirements and about one day of computation on a single computer for a relatively small dataset of up to 500,000 specimens.

Inertial wave turbulence, resulting from chaotic motions in enclosures filled with fluid, has been observed on the moons of Jupiter and is also present in lunar laser ranging on Earth. Researchers have been studying this phenomenon for over a decade, trying to understand its properties and behavior. A newly conducted experiment at the University of Washington adds a new layer of insight into inertial wave turbulence, verifying a previously theorized scaling of energy spectrum and providing a more precise measurement of the transition scale. The measured spectrum follows a Kolmogorov-like pattern, with the same exponent as turbulent fluids on Earth, while the transition scale was found to be proportional to the moon's angular velocity to the power of minus two, a relationship predicted by theories of inertial wave turbulence. The measured energy spectrum and transition scale also agree with computer simulations of turbulent inertial waves, further confirming the findings of the experiment.

This paper uses data from California's Inmate Sentence Completions (ISC) to examine the impact of mental health treatment within the prison system on recidivism rates among parolees. Previous research has shown that mental health issues are a primary factor in crime commission, with approximately one in five offenders struggling with a mental health disorder. Despite the significant role mental health plays in crime, there is a significant knowledge gap in understanding its effect on the criminal justice system. To bridge this knowledge gap, our research leverages a retrospective method that looks at the past criminal activities of individuals who have received mental health treatment within the prison system. Utilizing this approach, our results reveal that individuals who received mental health treatment within the prison system exhibit a 14-17% decrease in recidivism rates across various crime types, with the largest reduction seen in crimes against the person and property crimes. Notably, our findings demonstrate that mental health treatment has a more substantial effect on reducing recidivism in the categories of assault, burglary, and larceny than in other crime categories.

This study proposes a semi-supervised learning approach for medical image segmentation that utilizes an interpolation-based mixing technique. We hypothesize that labeling noise is random and follows a specific pattern and utilize this assumption to regularize the model's output. By employing an interpolation-based strategy, we convert labeled images into synthetic unlabeled data that the model can use during training. This approach serves as a form of data augmentation, and we leverage a specially designed network that generates high-quality synthetic data as an interpolation basis. We validate our method's efficacy by applying it to cardiac multi-label image segmentation and comparing it to established semi-supervised learning techniques.

To handle the significantly higher data rates expected from the Large Hadron Collider's upgraded sensors in its upcoming 2026 run, a new compact, high-speed digital system is being developed for the ATLAS Level1 Calorimeter Trigger. This system, known as jet FEX, will provide 1.09 Tbps of data processing and feature a compact, 6U 19-inch rack size. Initially built from off-the-shelf components, the prototype demonstrated 930 Gbps of data transfer and accuracy in 0.18 um CMOS technology. A fully custom, 16 nm CMOS design of the jet FEX system is now complete and has shown data transfer capabilities of up to 1.1 Tbps. This advanced design has been thoroughly tested and has already been integrated into the ATLAS LHC upgrade project.

Most current neural rendering approaches rely on tracking individual 3D points or inferring sparse 3D shapes to synthesize images. This is because estimating dense 3D models of multiple moving objects is too computationally demanding for a neural network. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a novel framework called Articulated Neural Rendering (ANR), which specifically addresses the challenge of rendering dynamic objects within dense, complex scenes. By incorporating a new module called the Articulated Neural Procedural Scene Module (ANPSM), ANR is capable of generating detailed 3D models comprising multiple articulations and occupancy modules. During inference, ANR uses bidirectional optimization to refine both the 3D model and rendering layers. In our experiments, we demonstrate that ANR surpasses state-of-the-art neural rendering methods by accurately rendering multiple moving objects, such as hands and faces, as well as complex scenes with various articulations, like jointed limbs in 3D models.

To gain deeper insights into materials dynamics, it's crucial to quantify the local atomic structure within materials. This task is complicated by the disordered nature of materials systems at the atomic level, making it difficult to pinpoint a single reference configuration. However, their microstructure often exhibits distinct, repeating patterns. By leveraging graph neural networks to analyze these patterns, we've developed a technique to represent materials' local atomic structures as unique invariants and apply it to two systems: nickel-aluminide nanowires and lithium in silicate glass. The method successfully identifies the prevalent atomic arrangements in nickel-aluminide nanowires, the distribution of Al impurities in lithium-aluminium clusters within lithium-aluminium nanowires, and the diverse local structures of lithium in silicate glass. Furthermore, we've observed a direct correlation between certain atomic configurations and lithium mobility in these glassy materials, which has significant implications for battery performance. This approach provides a powerful framework for uncovering hidden patterns in materials' local structures and can be used in conjunction with manipulation of atomic configurations to predict the effects of alterations to materials' microstructure.

This research supplements the findings related to weak convergence and function estimation that were outlined in Ghosh and Van Havere (2019). We provide an illustration of the concept in question using the context of count models, specifically Poisson models. We then establish the context in which non-parametric estimators can be used to approximate functions of parameters, and subsequently discuss the applicability of this approach to models that incorporate an extensive set of covariates.

The knowledge tracing task, which predicts students' future knowledge based on past performance, has gained significant interest and has been effectively addressed by deep learning methods in recent years. However, evaluating these models is a major obstacle due to the requirement of extensive real-world data. In an effort to address this challenge, researchers have proposed alternative assessment approaches that rely on substantially reduced synthetic datasets. However, these proposed evaluation methods have significant drawbacks, including model overfitting and the failure to account for data noise. Furthermore, there is a notable lack of studies that have compared the performance of these methods comprehensively. In response to these limitations, we have developed three synthetic evaluation methods for knowledge tracing models and conducted a comparative study, utilizing a comprehensive dataset of real-world student learning data. Our results show that the models can be evaluated accurately using these synthetic datasets, and that different evaluation methods are optimal for various types of knowledge tracing tasks. Our work represents a significant step towards standardizing the evaluation of knowledge tracing models.

We provide a detailed analysis of the relationship between surjectivity and injectivity for a class of second-order elliptic differential operators in the context of smooth functions, building on earlier work by Shaferv. Furthermore, our study offers a comprehensive framework that encompasses his findings. Within this framework, we specifically investigate the connection between the surjective and injective properties of such operators, as well as the implications of these properties for the inverse operator and the null space of the original differential operator. Our analysis involves an examination of the behavior of the operator's null space and the growth of its domain, as well as the structure of its inverse and surjectivity.

The veriT proof format has seen a marked evolution in its proof representation capabilities since its introduction at the PxTP workshop, reflecting veriT's growth as a versatile proof checker for many satisfiability modulo theories and first-order logic solvers. This survey showcases the various enhancements made to the format through its jury-driven development and highlights the diverse range of applications and research it has enabled in theorem proving and computational logic. Moreover, we highlight the notable achievements of the veriT verification and transformation tools developed to handle the complex proofs produced by the veriT solver. These advancements have been made possible by the ongoing collaboration among the veriT developers and the broader community, and have contributed significantly to the success of veriT in the field of satisfiability testing and logical reasoning.

FedBuff is a groundbreaking, privately implemented version of the Federated Averaging (FedAvg) algorithm that significantly boosts the scalability of a large number of users and reduces the need for costly cryptographic protocols in each user's iteration. Developed under a semi-honest quantum-resistant setup that employs the very efficient and widely adopted NIZK and NAEQ proof systems, the FedBuff algorithm allows a large and diverse group of users to participate in learning tasks with minimal data across multiple federated rounds. What sets FedBuff apart is its ability to create a reliable and secure aggregated update from the contributions of each user with minimal data, even when dealing with large and diverse datasets at scale. What prompted our investigation into FedBuff was the recognition that the existing private FedAvg implementations are either too inefficient for large-scale systems or too inflexible to accommodate various learning tasks. We formally prove the convergence rate of the FedBuff algorithm, both in theory and through practical applications, demonstrating its ability to achieve optimal learning performance in a wide range of scenarios, including multi-task and end-task learning, subject to certain conditions. What is particularly noteworthy about FedBuff is its ability to accommodate not only FedAvg but also other private federated learning algorithms, such as Private Federated Linear Regression via Jacobian aggregation, thereby providing a general framework for privately implementing any federated learning algorithm.

Using transfer learning, the performance of speech recognition systems can be significantly improved on languages with limited data, including those with significant differences in language structure, such as English and Japanese. However, transfer learning may also lead to speech recognition models being vulnerable to label inflation, a phenomenon where the accuracy improves more than expected with additional labels. In this study, we investigate the benefits and potential drawbacks of transfer learning for speech recognition on languages with varying levels of similarity, using a dataset that spans English, Spanish, and Japanese. Our results show that transfer learning can greatly improve performance between languages with some similarity, such as English and Spanish, but its benefits are less certain when the languages are less similar, such as English and Japanese. Additionally, we found evidence of label inflation in some of our experiments. We also explore alternative transfer learning techniques that converge more closely with the observed label inflation curve. Our findings suggest that transfer learning can be an effective tool for speech recognition on languages with some similarity, but its application and interpretation must be carefully considered.

This paper introduces a suite of novel node embedding techniques, along with
a comprehensive evaluation framework, for complex networks. Our node2graph2vec
library incorporates eight existing algorithms, including DeepGraph, DeepWalk,
GCN2vec, and GraphSAGE, and our experimental setup, encompassing metric-
based and sampling-based methods, enables thorough assessments of these methods.

An observation of a prominent structure in $B^{+}\to K^{+} K_S K_S$ decay spectrum around $m(K_S K_S)\sim 1.02$ GeV is reported. It is inferred that this structure's $S$-wave component is significantly larger than its $D$-wave component, with an overburden of more than five standard deviations. Additionally, a previous study's finding of a structure in $B^0\to K^0 K^0$ decay, also around $m(K_S K_S)\sim 1.02$ GeV, is confirmed with an overburden of over three standard deviations. By analyzing a 10.9 fb$^{-1}$ dataset of $pp$ collisions collected with the Belle II detector at the LHC, the study extracts $B^{+}\to K^{+} K_S K_S$ decay candidates, yielding 43,551 signal events after optimizations. A scan of the $K_S K_S$ mass spectrum reveals that the total width of this structure is wider than 140 MeV, and it constitutes at least 2.2$\times 10^{-5}$ of the $B^+$ decay rate.

The relationship between Primordial Black Hole Mass Accretion Rates and the total dark matter mass in the Universe remains an area of research, where a specific mass range of primordial black holes could account for 100% of dark matter if they form in large quantities, or could represent only a small portion of dark matter if they form individually. Analyzing LISA's sensitivity to these dark matter primordial black holes under two scenarios using a Genetic Algorithm, researchers found that LISA can distinguish between the two scenarios where primordial black holes make up all or just a part of the Universe's dark matter, as well as identify primordial black holes that form in large quantities and contribute 100% of dark matter, but may struggle with identifying those that form individually and contribute only a small portion of dark matter. Additionally, a more in-depth analysis of the case where primordial black holes make up all dark matter revealed that LISA can distinguish this scenario from other gravitational wave sources such as Compact Binary Mergers or a Population III Star Cluster.

Precise force measurement in series elastic actuators is crucial but complicated by nonlinearities and sensor limitations. This research presents a novel, adaptive method for estimating force that accounts for both elastic and sensor-related discrepancies. The proposed algorithm utilizes a general-purpose optimization technique and an innovative, adaptive scheduling method to balance measurement efficiency and accuracy. Key algorithmic parameters are optimized via evolutionary computation for minimum error, and the entire system is robustly validated using both simulation and actual testing of a designed elastic actuator setup.

By studying the breakup of a raft made up of particles that can change shape and flow, we've observed an unexpected pattern of cracks forming at specific distances from one another. These findings contradict the predictions made by existing theories that assume a static raft. We've developed an alternative explanation based on how the cracks progress, taking into account the competition between particles sticking together and the expansion of the fluid. Our model shows that the distance between adjacent cracks depends on the viscosity of the fluid and a time constant that reflects the interplay between particles and the flow. We've verified our findings by simulating and observing the rupture of rafts under tension, and our model has been applied to similar phenomena, such as the fragmentation of solid objects in turbulent fluid flows.

This study examines the electroweak symmetry-breaking phase transitions in lattice models that involve multiple complex scalar fields, using Monte Carlo simulations on the lattice. We analyze the multicomponent O(N)^d symmetric multicomponent O(N)^d symmetric theory for various values of d, where the symmetry is broken from O(N) to O(N-d). By exploring the low-temperature spectrum of the O(N) symmetry sector in the Monte Carlo simulations, we determine the critical behavior at these transition points. The results demonstrate that lattice simulations are an effective tool for studying the renormalization-group flow of continuum field theories, particularly in regions where renormalization-group scaling is disrupted. The findings in this study can be compared with the predictions of continuum field-theory studies that employ the effective potential approach, in order to validate the accuracy of this approach. The lattice simulations provide a transparent and unambiguous explanation for the observed symmetry-breaking phase transitions, in addition to illustrating the complex structure of the ground-state potential of the system.

Deep reinforcement learning structures can efficiently train policies for complex underwater missions, but they require extensive training data and slow learning curves, which can be challenging to model quickly. To accelerate this process, we've developed the SPGP-SARSA method, which uses a sparse grid to significantly reduce the number of required policy updates while maintaining fast learning. By only updating the most relevant grid points during policy evaluation, SPGP-SARSA significantly decreases the memory and computational costs. Our experiments show that SPGP-SARSA significantly outperforms traditional methods, such as SPGP and direct updates, in underwater navigation tasks, with a reduced memory footprint and faster learning curves.

This note confirms the findings of the paper "The Entanglement Pauli Group for qubits is not generated by the minimal sorting network" which appeared on the arXit e-print server under the title "Some Sorting Networks Are Not Generated by the Clifford+T Class". It first demonstrates that sorting networks of 2^d degrees for d=1 to 4 do do not belong to the Clifford+T universal quantum computing circuitry. It then shows that for d>1, networks of 2^(d+1) inputs or more are also capable of this same non-generation. It is worth noting that 2^(d+1) is the lowest known number for this capability, as a specific network of 6 nodes was previously shown to have this property in the referenced arXiv paper. It is also shown that the largest known circuit of this type which does not belong to the universal quantum computing circuitry is the well-known 4-qubit GHZ circuit, when degrees are taken into consideration. It is also confirmed that 3-qubit sorting networks of all degrees, as well as 4-qubit sorting networks of degrees 4 and 6, do belong to this universal quantum computing circuitry. It is also shown that any qubit entanglement circuit which only uses the Pauli operators, the Clifford+T universal quantum computing circuitry, and the Hadamard gate can be replicated by a sorting network of the same degrees in qubits of any number

By formulating a relativistic theory that incorporates one-fluid models within the framework of multisector theories, we have previously demonstrated the possibility of obtaining solutions for stellar objects that comprise two fluids by modifying single-fluid solutions. In this study, we reverse this procedure and aim to reverse-engineer one-fluid solutions from those with two fluids, with the additional constraint that the one-fluid solution must be consistent with the relativistic two-fluid model. We have developed three distinct strategies to achieve this goal for stellar objects in an asymptotically flat spacetime, and we have specifically applied each method to solve for isothermal relativistic stars under both the ideal and non-ideal cases.

Using high-resolution N-body simulations, this study investigates the impact of massive halo collisions on spiral galaxy disk evolution. Under normal conditions, a galactic disk evolves slowly due to its stable disk shape. However, a massive halo collision can trigger a bar formation in just one billion years through the disruption of the galactic disk's symmetry. This research examines how the composition of a galactic disk and its surrounding halo affects bar formation by simulating various collision scenarios. The results show that collisions resulting in massive halo material incorporation lead to bar formation, while those with a higher ratio of disk material lead to ring formation due to the additional angular momentum added to the disk. A comparison with existing research reveals a consistent finding: a higher ratio of disk to halo mass prevents bar formation. Additionally, the study finds that a larger scale length in a density distribution, such as the exponential disk model, facilitates bar formation. A new equation derived from the simulation shows the bar formation threshold in a galaxy's potential field is influenced by the ratio of its components, specifically $\frac{M_{\rm disk}}{M_{\rm bulge}}$ and $\frac{M_{\rm bulge}}{M_{\rm halo}}$, as well as the disk's rotation curve and angular momentum. This research also reveals the significant role halo collisions may play in the development of massive bars in galaxies like the Milky Way.

Both spiral galaxies and the Milky Way have weak magnetic fields due to which they lack the magnetic field patterns typical of disk galaxies. A comprehensive computer simulation investigates the effect of magnetic fields on galaxy mergers. Using advanced computer programs, the simulation models gas-rich galaxy mergers with magnetic fields similar to those found in spiral galaxies. The simulation consists of highly detailed simulations of gas, dust, and magnetic fields within multiple supercomputers. A pair of galaxies with similar masses are simulated in this computer experiment. The simulation begins with the galaxies approaching each other. As the galaxies merge, a massive spiral galaxy forms. Approximately 200 million years after the merger, a massive black hole with millions of times the mass of our sun is observed at the center of the galaxy. During the merger, both the galaxy and the black hole are affected by magnetic fields. However, the simulation shows that magnetic fields have little effect on the galaxy, the black hole, or the cosmic rays produced during the merger. The simulation also shows that magnetic fields cause the high-energy particles produced during the merger to be confined to the center of the galaxy, reducing the amount of cosmic rays that reach the black hole. The simulation shows that the accumulation of cosmic rays around the black hole powers massive cosmic ray outflows that can affect the galaxy and the surrounding intergalactic space. The simulation demonstrates the importance of magnetic fields in the behavior of cosmic rays during galaxy mergers.

To address the frequent issue of data imbalance in severity detection, we suggest a novel 3D contrastive learning approach known as the 3D Contrastive Mixup Classification (3DCMC) network. This proposal incorporates a contrastive learning mechanism called Contrastive Mixup Classification (CMC) for balanced classification. The 3DCMC network employs a Contrastive Mixup Attention Module (CMAM) that utilizes self-attention and CMC to rectify data imbalance. Moreover, it incorporates Residual Contrastive Mixup Blocks (RCMB) in the encoder layers to enhance robust feature extraction. Our experimental findings on the publicly accessible ADNI dataset demonstrate that the 3DCMC network achieves superior performance compared to current state-of-the-art techniques. Specifically, it exhibits higher accuracy, lower dice coefficients, and better robustness in the presence of data imbalance.

This study presents a novel GEC adaptation method that builds upon the
pre-existing knowledge of part-of-speech tagging. Our proposed method
demonstrates the effectiveness of cross-domain adaptation in GEC through the
integration of pre-trained models. Specifically, we utilize a multi-task
transfer learning approach that leverages the tagged input sentences.
Furthermore, we explore the incorporation of label-enforced masking to
further enhance the performance. Our proposed method achieves a notable gain of
4.13 and 3.19 points in F1-score on FAE and ParIC WIKI test sets,
respectively, when compared to the existing state-of-the-art methods.
Notably, our results indicate substantial improvements of 11.2 and 5.4 F1-score
points over traditional multi-task transfer learning approaches on FAE and
ParIC WIKI datasets, thereby establishing a new benchmark. The code and
preprocessed data are available for public access on our developed GitHub
repository.

In October 2018, a mental health emergency was declared in South Korea following a sudden spike in suicide cases. To gauge the effectiveness of the government's anti-suicide measures, new suicide data has been released but due to data protection policies, sensitive information has been rounded to the nearest five cases. This study investigates the impact of such data disclosure on statistical inference and explores the benefits of alternative data disclosure protocols. Notably, our findings indicate that rounding can significantly distort the results of inferential analysis, complicating the evaluation of the government's anti-suicide policies.

A study on GdInO3 thin films has been conducted, focusing on the structural, magnetic, and electrical characteristics. GdInO3 films were deposited on (001) LuScO3 substrants via pulsed laser deposition and calculated to be around 10 nm thick. An X-ray diffraction analysis revealed that the films possess a distorted rhombohedral Gd3+ ion lattice structure, likely attributed to oxygen deficiencies. The films exhibited a strong magnetic coupling with a spin canting angle of approximately 16.2 degrees, corresponding to an effective magnetic moment of 7.05 μB per Gd3+ ion. A high magnetic anisotropy constant (Kanis) was also observed, surpassing 10^6 erg/cm^3, and the metallic state was confirmed through I-V curve measurements.

In our research, we're examining a scenario where multiple agents compete to receive one out of several indistinguishable items. A fair allocation is the ultimate goal, and we're studying a round-robin based method where each agent takes turns assigning a positive fraction of an item to themselves or another agent. Our analysis shows that using this method results in an allocation that is at least an $\epsilon$-fairness fraction away from $1/N$-fairness compared to $1/\sqrt{n}$ for any constant $\epsilon$ when items are unbounded, and at least an $\epsilon$-fairness fraction away from $1/\sqrt{n}$-fairness when items are bounded. Furthermore, we're proving that using the cut-and-choose algorithm yields a $1/\sqrt{n}$-fairness allocation when items are unbounded, and an allocation that is at least an $\epsilon$-fairness fraction away from $1/N$-fairness when items are bounded.

We challenge the conventional approach to pseudo-labeling a target image using multiple translated versions, instead proposing that averaging these translations produces a more effective and robust target pseudo-label. Our key insight is that low-quality translations contaminate the pseudo-labeling process, masking their presence would allow the model to focus on the target to be learned. We develop an iterative pseudo-labeling technique that leverages translation diversity, starting with a coarse pseudo-label and refining it by iterating between generating diverse translations and fine-tuning on the top-performing ones using a hard example loss. Our experiments demonstrate that this approach, which we call Multi-Translation Pseudo-Labeling, achieves superior performance on target tasks, particularly when the source domain data is limited, outperforming strong baselines by over 10\% in certain scenarios.

We present an in-depth analysis of HII regions within the galaxy UGC 8839, 
an edge-on spiral galaxy. Using data from the CALIFA spectroscopic database, 
we identify HII regions through their optical emission spectra, correcting for 
foreground extinction. A total of 121 HII regions were detected and analyzed, 
which were then modeled to determine their spatial orientation, star formation 
rates, and distances from the galaxy center. By classifying these HII regions 
according to their radii from the galaxy center, we observed a significant shift 
in the ages of HII regions, with older regions residing in the outer radii and 
younger regions in the inner radii. We also found evidence of a barry structure 
within the galaxy's central region and a significant increase in the star formation 
rate in this area. The distribution of HII regions across the galaxy shows a 
maximum in the central structure and a slight alignment with the major axis. 
The results of this analysis provide a comprehensive understanding of the UGC 
8839 galaxy's structure and evolution.

Researchers propose a novel method for detecting dark matter, known as paleo-detection, which involves searching for evidence of dark matter interactions within ancient radioactive decay patterns recorded in fossils and meteorites. Since dark matter nucleon interactions are likely lowest at very low mass scales, it's essential to investigate this range. By examining the half-lives of various radioactive isotopes, including $^{41}$K and $^{79}$Se, whose half-lives can be affected by dark matter interactions, a team developed a detection method. The team analyzed the isotope $^{41}$K, which is of interest for particle accelerators, to find any signs of dark matter influence. To accomplish this, the experts created a statistical analysis method that compares observed deviations from expected half-lives with those generated by simulations of dark matter interactions at various mass scales. This method allows for the derivation of upper limits on dark matter interaction probabilities at specific mass ranges. Through simulation of data that could be obtained from future particle accelerator and direct dark matter detection experiments, the researchers anticipate that paleo-detection could provide a complementary perspective on dark matter interactions at very low mass scales, potentially surpassing the sensitivity of existing experiments in the mass range of 10 to 100 eV.

Modern databases managing sensitive user data frequently require the publication of updated datasets, posing a security risk due to the disclosure of sensitive information. A notorious threat involves attackers inferring sensitive updates from database publication history. Notably, adversaries can be deterred from such access by utilizing differential privacy, a well-established concept. However, implementing differential privacy across a broad database update history presents significant computational challenges. We present an innovative technique for privately releasing a database update history in real-time, addressing scalability issues through the incorporation of a flexible linear combination of log likelihood ratios. This incorporated method is shown to maintain differential privacy at a computationally manageable cost, making it suitable for practical application and demonstrated through a data-set involving Twitter user updates.

Understanding why a machine learning model makes incorrect predictions is crucial for its effectiveness. Minimally unsatisfiable cores, a previously underutilized concept, holds significant potential for this insight. Previously, incorporating unsatisfiability analysis into feature importance assessment required substantial computational time. A recent advancement, though, has reduced this time to a fraction of the original. Our work builds upon existing research, combining the application of minimal unsatisfiable cores to 9th DIMACS Challenge problems and recent computational optimizations. We conducted these experiments under modern conditions, using a current SAT solver, to determine the actual performance improvement. Consequently, our findings demonstrate an average 6-fold speed increase across all 9 problems on a contemporary computer.

This paper introduces a novel Deep Learning framework, known as Dual Decoder Attention Network (DDANet), which utilizes attention mechanisms in both encoding and decoding layers to create a Dual Path network. We incorporate multiple convolutional layers in the encoding path and a deconvolutional layer in the decoding path to achieve image segmentation. The Dual Path network allows for the sharing of learned features between encoder and decoder layers, which enhances the segmentation of a challenging task like automating the detection of surgical instruments. Our research indicates that DDANet yields superior results in comparison to Convolutional Neural Network (CNN), U-Net, and Fully Convolutional Network (FCN), with an overall accuracy rating of 85.6%, outperforming the baseline methods by 8.2%, 5.5%, and 4.3% respectively. Additionally, our method demonstrates comparable performance to Recurrent Attention Network (RANet) with an overall accuracy of 84.3%.

Recent unsupervised ReID methods integrate contrastive learning as a primary technique but tend to overlook the underlying data structures, resulting in reduced learning effectiveness due to label lag. Moreover, existing contrastive learning approaches overlook the inherent label correlations, resulting in the failure to fully tap into the method's potential. To address these limitations, this research integrates graph neural networks and contrastive learning to extract feature representations and enforce label structures, ultimately improving the performance of unsupervised ReID. Our proposed framework, UGCL, leverages a unified two-layer structure consisting of GCL and a contrastive learning module, where each layer is designed to learn distinct aspects of data structures and label correlations. To achieve this, UGCL incorporates two contrastive learning approaches: a global contrastive learning approach to extract global feature representations based on identity information and a local contrastive learning approach to enforce label structures and eliminate noise. Our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of UGCL, outperforming state-of-the-art unsupervised ReID methods across three benchmarks. The code is available at: \url{https://github.com/hiyixing/UGCL}.

This study presents a novel, integrated approach that combines GARCH-based modeling with external information for forecasting Value-at-Risk (VaR). Unlike conventional GARCH models, our approach continuously updates its parameters in response to new information, resulting in a more effective and reliable VaR forecasting method. Leveraging the strengths of Extreme Value Theory (EVT), we develop a generalized return distribution that accounts for both frequent and extreme returns, enabling computation of the VaR. Our proposed framework, in contrast to standard approaches, continuously updates its parameters using the Exponential Weighted Moving Average (EWMA) method. We utilize historical data for 30 major stock market indices across the globe to evaluate and compare our method to traditional GARCH and EWMA models, finding that the vaR forecasts from our approach exhibit lower errors and a more accurate coverage probability than the traditional GARCH model. Notably, our results show that our approach outperforms GARCH and EWMA models in 70% and 10% of cases respectively, as measured by the CRPS error. Additionally, our approach demonstrates a higher coverage probability than the traditional GARCH model in 85% of cases.

Multiple pulsar timing array data sets are combined to detect minute deviations in gravitational waves, resulting in vast multidimensional datasets that require sophisticated sampling methods. This study compares the performance of forward model sampling, nested sampling, and parallelised ensemble sampling on a PAraTime Array Data, evaluating the accuracy of its model and sampling uncertainties. The case study involves the IoA's PTA dataset, incorporating data from 49 pulsars and spanning nearly 10 years, with findings that ensemble sampling excels in efficiency and nested sampling excels in precision. However, further research is needed to perfect the ensemble sampling algorithm. This work is openly available at https://github.com/hpcnz/PTA-sampling.

Using lattice QCD through a quasi-continuum approach, this study examines how the properties of pions are affected by variations in quark masses at different spatial scales. The analysis is performed for Nf=2, 2+1 flavor ensembles generated by the IFAE@IFC collaboration for a range of quark mass values. The findings indicate that the ratio of the pion decay constant to the quark mass exhibits little scale dependence, primarily influenced by chiral symmetry breaking effects at shorter distances. In contrast, the pion mass is significantly more susceptible to the choice of quark mass at larger scales, with connections to the sigma meson mass and dark matter properties.

The extreme variability in classical T Tauri stars' accretion rates poses an evolutionary puzzle, with their disks evolving from a protracted phase of intense accretion. P-TeP, a newly discovered variable T Tauri star, exhibits exceptionally extreme variability in its H$\alpha$ profile, comprising four distinct phases of varying accretion patterns over a two-year period. From spectroscopic calculations of the ionizing flux, we observe that P-TeP's accretion variability spans from minimal to extremely high levels of hot spot radiation, sufficient to account for up to 98% of the H$\alpha$ continuum, indicating a significant shift in the balance of hot spot and chromospheric contributions. The spectrum of P-TeP transformed from a purely accretion-driven H$\alpha$ profile to one dominated by chromospheric activity, and the star's magnetic field likely regulates the reprocessing of its disk's energy, shifting between hot spot and chromospheric dominance. The extreme variability in the H$\alpha$ profile of P-TeP offers a pivotal example of the dynamic balance that can exist in the interaction between the magnetic field, chromosphere, and accretion streams, a phenomenon that can be a product of extremely variable internal disk accretion, as seen in P-TeP, or the external influence of a massive interacting stellar system, as seen in the case of V929 Orionis.

This paper presents an economic model that allows us to examine public reactions to redistribution in response to fortune's influence on social mobility and income. We distinguish between two fortune scenarios: one where good luck opens up new career opportunities, and another where good luck predicts high income regardless of career choices. We find that people are generally more supportive of increased redistribution and a more comprehensive safety net when fortune's impact is directly on income, as it creates stronger intuition that individual effort is less responsible. In contrast, people are less supportive of these policies when fortune's effect is on opportunities, as this triggers a greater intuition of personal responsibility. These findings are consistent with survey data and are reflected in how people assess responsibility across these scenarios. The model further shows that people are more inclined to view success due to luck as undeserved, as well as more inclined to view failure as unpredictable rather than unfair. These results have implications for designing policy messaging and the provision of public services.

Building on the foundation of 'The quantum Euler characteristic of stable maps', this study further develops the concept of Euler characteristics for higher-dimensional varieties corresponding to stable maps under the influence of quantum $K$-invariants in the framework of 'Categorical quantum $K$-theory'. Specifically, this work establishes the relationship between these Euler characteristics and quantum $K$-invariants, while also providing the formula for the Euler characteristics in question. Additionally, this study introduces a functor $\chi_{\mathfrak{t}}^{\mathfrak{s}}(\tau)$ from the space of stability conditions to the ring of functions on the torus, which serves as a fundamental component in the study of quantum $K$-theory and its connections to derived categories. This paper also outlines the steps for computing $\chi_{\mathfrak{t}}^{\mathfrak{s}}(\tau)$ for a variety $X$, by describing the source category $\mathcal{C}^{\mathfrak{s}}(\tau)$, and exploring the connection between $\chi_{\mathfrak{t}}^{\mathfrak{s}}(\tau)$ and $\chi_{\mathfrak{t}}(\tau')$ for isomorphic stability conditions.

DeepLearning systems rely heavily on data, with poor quality data posing a significant threat to their performance. As AI systems become more complex, it's increasingly difficult to identify and rectify data issues manually. We're introducing DataScope, an automated data debugging tool that speeds up the process by pinpointing and fixing flawed data by itself. DataScope works seamlessly with existing training pipelines and pinpointing tools, and its innovative features include customizable data quality specifications, a data validation engine, a debugging planner, and a data fixing framework. By efficiently identifying and fixing data issues, DataScope can significantly reduce the time required for data debugging, a major improvement over traditional manual approaches. Through comprehensive tests on real-world datasets, DataScope has demonstrated its capability to accelerate data debugging by at least 5-10 times across various machine learning applications.

Researchers examined 13 globular clusters within the 15 GHz VLA survey area to identify radio sources within the clusters' cores. This study yielded seven new radio sources within the cores of six globular clusters. Five of these sources were associated with known millisecond pulsar X-ray binaries: XUMC 1820-303 (Ter5), XUMC 2034-424 (Ter5), XUMC 2134-442 (Ter5), X3UMC 1839-303 (Ter5), and XUMC 2059-360 (NGC 6404). One of these X-ray binaries was discovered through radio detection alone. Another source, XUMC 2048-363 (NGC 6404), is an unidentified radio source that may be a neutron star or a cluster member with an alternative radio emission pattern.

When analyzing graph data, a method called hypergraph reconstruction is used to create a detailed representation of a complex network based on a set of related nodes identified within individual graphs. A recent study developed an efficient algorithm for this task by assuming the underlying hypergraph takes the form of a k-uniform K_n structure. However, the researchers have now expanded on this work by testing the algorithm's performance with more general k-uniform and large n sizes. The results show the successful recovery of the hypergraph when it has a relatively low edge density, but the algorithm struggles with more dense structures. The challenges posed by hidden nodes and their connections within the hypergraph also hinder the reconstruction process. The studies conducted a thorough examination of the algorithm's limitations and potential extensions, as well as explored alternative methods for its implementation.

The emission direction of a laser is considered a key characteristic that varies depending on the type of laser and operating conditions. However, measuring emission directionality is a complex process, involving sophisticated measurements and sophisticated data analysis. Researchers have previously assumed a Gaussian beam model, which has limitations when dealing with far-field data. In response to these challenges, a new method has been developed to infer emission directionality from laser spectra in the laboratory and in space. This approach uses minimum support Bayesian techniques in combination with mathematical transformations of the data, resulting in more accurate results that also consider uncertainties. By applying this method to laboratory measurements of two different types of lasers and in-flight measurements of the HIBARF laser, researchers were able to determine the emission directionality of these lasers for the first time. The results showed that the emission directionality of these lasers is much narrower than previously assumed, with values of $\phi_{1/e} < 0.16$ and $\theta_{1/e} < 0.54$ for the HIBARF laser in flight. These precise measurements of emission directionality will significantly improve the accuracy of internal energy measurements in laboratory and space experiments.

In this paper, we examine the interaction between coherent light and a group of atoms in motion, specifically within a one-dimensional system where atoms are positioned at regular intervals along a line. We define a two-time second-order correlation function for the electromagnetic field, which arises from the collective effect of atoms moving past a reference point. By considering the perspective of an observer moving with the same velocity as the atoms, we can tie the correlation function to the properties of the electromagnetic field in the rest frame. We then use this connection to derive the spectrum of light observed as a result of scattering, and demonstrate how it relates to the Wigner-Villers function, which we graph for various velocity ranges. These calculations yield a Lorentzian-shaped spectrum, and the width of this shape is determined by the movement of the atoms.

In offline learning scenarios for multiple agents interacting, the usual assumption that data varies based on the learner and includes noisy data and diverse samples poses significant challenges. Our novel Shared Individual Trajectories (SIT) framework addresses these difficulties by presenting a method for agents to learn from unique offline data sets, leveraging the underlying shared structure. By employing shared representations and exploiting differences in individual data, we can derive precise policy targets and multiply the benefits of offline learning. Our approach on top of the TRPO algorithm significantly enhances the learning capabilities in complex State-Action-Reward spaces, outperforming baseline methods by up to 5 times in various Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning scenarios, including fully connected graphs and cooperative grid world scenarios.

A new CNN-based method is introduced for bidirectional image registration, leveraging deep learning, in this study. Unlike conventional methods that focus on matching image intensities, this approach directly compares feature maps generated by encoding input images as codes. Primarily, an optimal transformation is found by minimizing a discrepancy metric between code pairs, using cyclical siamese networks. What sets this method apart is its ability to perform registration in both directions, without the need for additional training, by exploiting symmetry in network architecture. Experiments demonstrate that this proposed framework surpasses state-of-the-art techniques in brain MR image registration accuracy.

Single-particle entanglement has unique characteristics that distinguish it from nonlocal correlations in multi-particle settings. A single-particle entanglement measure has been developed that applies to both discrete and continuous settings, and demonstrates its own distinctive nonlocal impact on quantum steering and the Heisenberg uncertainty principle. Through explicit examples and simulations, it is shown that this measure alone is insufficient to capture the full extent of nonlocal effects in multi-particle systems, and that single-particle entanglement can coexist with substantial correlations in multi-particle settings. Furthermore, single-photon entanglement with a massive object has been demonstrated in an optical interferometer system, realizing single-particle entanglement in a symmetrized state.

The integration of vehicles, infrastructure, and data into a unified system, as envisioned by the Internet of Vehicles (IoV), creates numerous opportunities and challenges. With the increasing amount of sensitive data being generated, there's a growing need to ensure data security and privacy. Traditional security measures have proven ineffective, and IoV's complex and dynamic environment demands a more sophisticated and adaptable approach. Our research focuses on leveraging Blockchain technology to enhance data security and privacy within the IoV ecosystem. We first examine the current state of IoV architectures, applications, and security challenges. Then, we explore various Blockchain technologies and their potential applications in the IoV ecosystem, identifying suitable platforms and use cases such as secure data sharing, payment systems, and traffic management. We also delve into the development of a IoV architecture that integrates Blockchain and a microservices architecture, emphasizing scalability, efficiency, and flexibility. Our proposed architecture is then applied to create several secure and privacy-preserving services, including a data sharing platform and payment system, utilizing popular Blockchain platforms such as Hyperledger Fabric and Ethereum. Our results demonstrate high performance, achieving throughputs of up to 1000 transactions per second, along with low latency and efficient resource utilization. Our work contributes to the advancement of the IoV ecosystem, providing secure, privacy-preserving, and scalable services that can accommodate diverse applications and infrastructure, paving the way for the seamless integration of vehicles, infrastructure, and data, and creating a robust foundation for the development of secure and innovative IoV

The rare observation of a nova in its post-eruption phase with spectral lines in its natural state allows us to study the impact of the eruption on the binary system. By analyzing the optical data from the VShSpectrograph at the SAAO 1.9m telescope, we observed V392 Persei three years after its eruption in 2018. By comparing the spectra to those of similar systems, we found that the absorption line profiles in V392 Persei's post-eruption phase are similar to those of systems with similar white dwarf masses. This suggests that the nova eruption did not significantly alter the binary system's mass transfer habits. Nonetheless, the system showed an increased synthesis rate of helium enrichment products, suggesting that the nova eruption may have disrupted the equilibrium between the binary system's energy release and mass transfer. This disruption might be temporary, and we propose that future observations, particularly during the maximum brightness of the orbital period, may provide further insight into the binary system's behavior and the effects of the nova eruption.

To assess the competence of individual quantum gates within a quantum computing array, several experiments utilize highly entangled states like the toric code, which serves as a stringent benchmark.  In this study, a simulation is employed to evaluate the impact of imperfect quantum gates on toric code states generated via a sequence of gate applications.  Both classical and quantum gate failures are investigated, with focus on the duration of stability for detectable topological quantum error correction.  A novel inspection tool is developed to analyze the dynamics of these states through application of the Fisher information criterion, enabling the identification of threshold magnitudes for both classical and quantum gate imprecision.  The findings of this study are verified via NISQ devices.

This paper introduces an innovative feedback encoding technique that allows for efficient codebook design in a wireless communication system, reducing pilot overhead. By training neural networks at the base station and the mobile device, we leverage a generative adversarial network to create a codebook that minimizes interference between users. Each mobile device can then learn a personalized codebook for reduced pilot sessions, resulting in an optimized feedback encoding scheme. Our proposed method outperforms traditional clustering methods, such as K-means, by producing superior performance with significantly less pilot overhead. Furthermore, the proposed method achieves superior performance compared to fixed codebook approaches in scenarios with mobile devices.

We investigate Dirac cones on the surface of semi-imaginary quartic massless Dirac fermion models in $3+1$ dimensions, representing a fictional analogue of the $\mathcal{K}3$ surface. Our study shows that these Dirac cones are protected through topological arguments and discrete symmetries within two distinct scenarios. Firstly, we demonstrate that surface currents, which display persistent and localized chiral flow, are inherently robust across both bosonic and fermionic systems. Secondly, we establish that these surface Dirac cones cannot be transformed into higher-order dispersion relations associated with surface modes in $3+1$ dimensions. Our analysis further reveals that the $\mathcal{K}3$ surface, representing a four-dimensional analogue of the torus, can give rise to surface modes with $\mathcal{C}2$ symmetry, which we illustrate through the construction of a pseudo-fermion model. This pseudo-fermion model then enables us to examine the topological surface states in the AdS$_5$ spacetime, specifically the anti-holomorphic fermion on the $\mathcal{K}3$ surface within the $N4$ SCFT system, which corresponds to an $N=4$ supersymmetric Yang-Mills theory with gauge group $SU(N)$.

This study examines the Brans-Dicke theory to determine the requirements for photons to reach null infinity, focusing on the impact of scalar gravitational waves. We establish a key invariant $I$ that measures the curvature caused by gravitational waves and calculate its effect on the near-null infinity behavior of photons. Specifically, we show that if the initial data satisfies specific decay rate criteria, with the exception of the impact of scalar waves, it is sufficient for photons to escape to null infinity. Conversely, a suitable choice of initial data can result in photons behaving in a manner that prevents escape to null infinity. Moreover, we explore the relationship between the choice of coordinates and the appearance of singularities in the vicinity of null infinity, and demonstrate that the inherent existence of future null infinity in the physical spacetime is a non-coordinatization issue.

The LISA will detect numerous stellar-mass binary black hole (BBH) mergers due to Population III binary remnants. To determine the diversity of these events, we must understand the characteristics of Population III stars and how they influence the formation of BBH systems. Assuming that all relevant massive stellar populations contain exactly one massive, non-variable superstar, we can use the time available for systems to form before the universe becomes too transparent due to CMB fluctuations as an indicator of when systems can form. Using this, we find that all relevant massive stellar populations produce systems that can be detected by LISA, with the merger rate density peaking at a 2.5 times the current redshift and accounting for nearly the entire detected BBH population. What primarily limits the abundance of these systems is the scarcity of zero-metallicity stars rather than the scarcity of massive stars. Systems formed post-redshift of 7 also fail to provide sufficient merger rates due to the insufficient abundance of low-mass BBH systems. Systems composed of two 10-solar-mass stars in a binary system produce mergers that peak at higher redshifts. What primarily limits the abundance of these systems is the scarcity of zero-metallicity stars rather than the scarcity of massive stars. A new software simulator for gamma-ray bursts has been developed, allowing for the realistic generation of time and energy variations typical of GRBs encountered by the Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope. The team designed the simulator to assess the performance of the Fermi Gamma-ray Burst Monitor's burst detection and localization algorithms during spaceflight. By simulating the monitor's onboard observations and data processing procedures in real-time, the simulator can determine the detection and localization outcomes of GRBs. The simulator's time and energy characteristics are accurately replicated, with a time-jitter addition that is consistent with the natural variations found in GRBs. The system was tested on a computer cloud using up to 128 processing cores and showed excellent scalability. The simulator can generate 1000 bursts per hour for a typical two-year mission duration, providing a large dataset of 18 million GRB simulations. These simulations include all types of GRBs, from weak events that are below the monitor's detection threshold to extremely bright events that are nearly identical to the monitor's top 10 brightest detections. The simulator's performance and large dataset of burst simulations make it an invaluable tool for testing the Fermi/GBM burst detection and localization algorithms during the spaceflight phase.

For 1 < p $\le$ 2, consider the space BMOA_p of analytic functions on the unit disk that extend analytically to the upper half-plane and whose boundary values belong to the F^p(BMO) space. A compact operator, T_g, is defined as a composition of the Cauchy transform with a G_z function, where G_z is an almost periodic function in H^1. The paper investigates the compactness of T_g on BMOA_p, demonstrating that this property holds for a non-degenerate range of G_z functions in BMOA_p spaces. Additionally, a characterization of weakly compact operators is obtained for a larger range of BMOA_p than previously known, and this characterization is based on a Volterra-type operator or a composition of the Cauchy transform with almost periodic functions in H^1 with a specific discontinuity property.

Understanding how knowledge evolves over time is crucial in navigating the vast and ever-expanding body of scientific literature. Deep learning methods have significantly improved in processing simple knowledge but struggle with complex, nuanced knowledge. Quantitative indices of knowledge, such as the Quantitative Index of Knowledge (KQI), are essential in measuring knowledge evolution and providing valuable insights into the flow of knowledge within scientific literature. However, current KQI methods are largely tailored to process text-based scientific literature and fail to accommodate multimedia knowledge. Moreover, they lack the capability to capture knowledge from a multimodal perspective. To address these limitations, we introduce a novel framework called Multi-Modal Quantitative Index of Knowledge (M$^2$KIQI) that leverages deep learning techniques to extract knowledge from image, text, and audio datasets, thereby enabling the comprehensive analysis of multimedia knowledge. Our approach comprises multiple components, including data representation, correlation analysis, and normalization to compute the multimodal distribution of points, followed by calculation of the KQI. Empirical evaluations conducted on a range of multimedia datasets serve as proof of concept for our framework.

This study examines the security risks associated with a wireless communication network consisting of multiple access points and various data transmission nodes, employing a technique called double layer secure transmission. We developed and operationalized a maximization problem to increase the minimum security level among all nodes, constrained by factors including power usage, network topology, and data transmission protocols. By leveraging an algorithm that refines initial guesses, we were able to find efficient solutions to this complex problem. Notably, our results under real-world simulation scenarios outperformed existing methods known as DGM and SF, while also providing secure transmission as a key factor in optimization.

Quantum emitters have shown great promise for the development of non-local entangled states in complex photonic networks. To achieve this, we propose a novel scheme that takes advantage of topologically protected edge states in non-Hermitian systems. Specifically, we investigate a photonic wire with non-Hermitian resonators arranged in an alternating pattern of Hermitian and anti-Hermitian units. Due to their non-Hermitian nature, this system exhibits unique properties, such as magnetic translation symmetry and parity-time symmetry, which are responsible for creating pairs of non-Hermitian localized states at the network terminals. Utilizing optical resonators with coupled photonics, we demonstrate how to control the emission dynamics of these edge states by incorporating quantum emitters into the network. By properly tuning the emitters' frequencies and coupling strengths, we show that we can create quantum emitters that not only replicate the non-Hermitian localized states but also entangle with them. This entanglement is evidenced by photonic simulations using the Luescher algorithm. This proposal offers an optical realization of an entangled state protected by symmetries present only in non-Hermitian systems.

This research focuses on the trajectory planning aspects of connected and automated vehicles as they approach urban intersections. A key factor influencing this trajectory is the wait time dictated by traffic signals, which significantly affects the coordination between vehicles and infrastructure. Given the variability in traffic signals, this study develops a novel prediction framework to estimate wait times, curve characteristics, and potential cuts based on real-world data from the US and Europe. This prediction framework is designed to be both data-efficient and robust. To evaluate the performance of this framework, the developed models are tested using real-world traffic data from different locations, and the results show a high degree of accuracy with minimal requirements for computational power. This research demonstrates the effectiveness of its proposed methods as the vehicle approaches an intersection, and it is compatible with a more advanced trajectory planning framework called TimeToTarget.

We introduce a new fast text-based game simulator called TextWorldExpress, 
which significantly accelerates the generation of text-based games by increasing 
the size of state and action representations while maintaining solvability and 
consistency. Our method called XSimpleGenerator creates these extended game 
descriptions in TextWorldExpress by expanding initial scenarios with basic 
objects, actions, and commands. We show that existing advanced game generators 
fail to solve many TextWorldExpress puzzles due to their slow processing and 
limited ability to handle large game states. In contrast, our TextWorldExpress 
demonstrates a notable increase in gameplay complexity with 5-10 times larger 
grid sizes, unusual action combinations, and intricate instruction support. 
Notably, generating a single TextWorld challenge under these conditions takes 
less than 1 second on a single CPU, a feat that cannot be achieved by our 
previous state-of-the-art model, the SimpleTextWorldGenerator, which requires 
multiple GPUs and takes over 1000 times longer.

Deep learning techniques have rapidly emerged as the standard for various computing tasks, largely due to their exceptional accuracy. However, their massive memory and processing demands have created significant obstacles for widespread adoption, particularly in resource-constrained devices. To address this limitation, researchers have explored the integration of deep learning models with tensor decomposed techniques that take advantage of specialized hardware. For example, the High-Performance Extensible Tensor Core (HPETC) was designed to accelerate matrix and tensor operations, resulting in a 4-5 times increase in throughput and up to 8 times improvement in energy efficiency. Building upon the successful application of recurrent neural networks (RNNs), this study extends the HPETC hardware capability to other deep learning models, the long short-term memory network (LSTM) in particular. The proposed FDHT-LSTM architecture leverages the HPETC's matrix and tensor processing features, achieving a 2.5-3.5 times boost in throughput and 5-7 times improvement in energy efficiency compared to a software-based implementation, as validated through extensive benchmarking using the DeepBurn benchmark suite. Furthermore, the FDHT-LSTM architecture was found to provide a 20-30% increase in accuracy over its software-based and tensor-decomposed model-oriented hardware counterparts.

To accelerate training NLP models, various data augmentation techniques have been developed in recent years, offering a balanced approach between data and computational resources. While some methods focus on word-level alterations, this study explores more comprehensive data augmentation strategies on sentence and sequence-levels. We investigate the efficiency of different data augmentation techniques, combining nine distinct methods including simple token rearrangements to more complex synthetic data generation using conditional language models. Experiments conducted on nine NLP tasks demonstrate that data augmentation is a universally applicable solution for enhancing model performance, with the simplicity of sentence-level data augmentation often outperforming more complex methods. Additionally, our findings show that data augmentation can be optimized through task selection and that a carefully curated all-task model achieves state-of-the-art results on eight out of nine evaluated tasks.

A new, more fundamental formulation of the Weak Gravity Conjecture is examined in this study, specifically in anti-de Sitter space. It is hypothesized that a class of charged particles with a certain self-binding energy below a specific threshold cannot exist within the space. To validate this formulation, an existence proof is required for a pair of charged particles with a self-binding energy greater than this threshold in anti-de Sitter space. This existence proof can be used to demonstrate that a certain class of highly charged black holes are unable to exist in this space. The formulation can also be applied to a scalar field with a certain symmetry to show that a class of charged particles with this symmetry cannot exist in anti-de Sitter space. This research builds upon previous findings by Gubser, Pomeransky, and Syresin that demonstrated the non-existence of certain pairs of charged particles with this self-binding property in anti-de Sitter space near the boundary. The new existence proofs can be applied to charged particles located at a distance from the boundary.

By incorporating an adaptive multi-configurational time-dependent wavefunction model, our method accelerates the calculation of excited states in simulations. This approach leverages an extensive set of reference wavefunctions to precisely describe multiple quantum states of distinct energies. As the size of these simulations expands, directly determining reference wavefunctions through the time-dependent Ritz method becomes impractically time-consuming. In contrast, our model-space approach efficiently identifies the required reference wavefunctions by running the time-dependent Ritz method on a much smaller set of starting candidates, thus significantly cutting down the calculation time. We demonstrate this improvement through a series of challenges posed by dynamic processes involving nonadiabatic electronic transitions, wavefunction mixing under intense laser pulses, and electron correlation in laser-driven atoms.

Given a local ring R with an idempotent element f, we investigate the properties of a specific zero submodule of the local cohomology module $\displaystyle\mathsf{H}^i_{\mathfrak{m}}(R,f)$ when $i=1$. We demonstrate that this zero submodule is generated by the $R$-module $\displaystyle\frac{N^1_R}{f\frac{N^1_R}{f}}$, which has been previously recognized as a rationality parameter in the study of Noetherian local rings. Additionally, we establish connections between this zero submodule and other measures of F-rationality, including the Castelnuovo-Mumford regularity and the Auslander-Buchsbaum inequality. These investigations provide new insights into the relationship between zero submodules of local cohomology and F-rationality, which have been initially explored in our earlier work with Schenck and Vascellari.

The integration of variable renewable energies into the grid requires the development of efficient redispatch markets, with a specialized module for optimal coordination. Current studies on order design, origin-destination networks, and stochastic models are already exploring this concept, but there is a lack of research on the optimal design of all-or-none orders in a simple one-sided market model. Our study investigates the effects of introducing all-or-none orders on the grid operator's procurement behavior and finds that they can significantly reduce the social cost, but only if the market share of all-or-none orders is below a certain threshold. Furthermore, we analyze the strategic response of generators and aggregators in a multi-type, multi-type competition scenario, and derive conditions under which all-or-none orders can exclude traditional orders as a dominant strategy. Our results demonstrate that the optimal design features an infinite number of types, with specific characteristics, and implies a first-price auction mechanism for all-or-none orders, which induces an equilibrium without collusion. Finally, we validate our theoretical findings with numerical simulations.

In this work, we demonstrate that a vast majority of Galois groups associated with irreducible polynomials over finite fields exhibit maximal complexity, specifically that a vast majority of such polynomials possess Galois groups that are highly transitive or super-natural. This finding is integral to a significant extension of the Bateman-Horn Conjecture in the context of function fields.

To study the impact of top quark pair generation on Higgs boson signal detection at future $pp$ colliders, we examine top quark decay to lighter fermions instead of $b\bar{b}$. We modify MadGraph5\_aMC@NLO to account for this decay mode and simulate its effect at the LHC and future $pp$ colliders. We find that, even with the top quark pair resonance in place, the presence of this additional decay channel has a negligible impact on Higgs boson signal detection. Conversely, at the LHC, even without the top quark pair resonance, this decay mode has a negligible impact on Higgs boson signal detection. However, at the LHC, even without the top quark pair resonance, this decay mode has a negligible impact on Higgs boson signal detection. However, at future $pp$ colliders with $\sqrt{s} = 100\,TeV$, this decay mode causes the $t\bar{t}$ cross section to rise above the Standard Model prediction, significantly reducing the signal-to-background ratio for the $\phi\to b\bar{b}$ decay mode. To mitigate this effect, we propose a series of searches for the $\phi\to WZ\to \ell\ell b\bar{b}$ decay mode, which are resilient to the top quark pair background.
